utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Brady. As the Registrar announced, the case we are hearing today is the Prosecutor against Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic. Mr. Vasiljevic is appearing against the judgement issued by Trial Chamber II of this Tribunal on the 29th of November, 2002. The Trial Chamber convicted Mr. Vasiljevic on two of the ten counts charged by the Prosecution: First, on Count 3 of the indictment, for persecution as a crime against humanity; for the murder of five Muslim men and the inhumane acts inflicted on two other Muslim men during the Drina River incident. This conviction was entered under Article 5 of the Tribunal's Statute. Second, the Trial Chamber convicted Mr. Vasiljevic on Count 5, for murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war for the murder of five Muslim men during the Drina River incident. This conviction is pursuant to Article 3 of the Statute. The Trial Chamber acquitted Mitar Vasiljevic on the remaining charges. Mr. Vasiljevic was sentenced to a single sentence of imprisonment for 20 years. The Prosecutor did not appeal against the trial judgement. Before hearing the parties' arguments, I will summarise the grounds of appeal presented by Mr. Vasiljevic in his written submissions. The appellant's written submissions were not always well structured and several arguments were repeated under more than one ground of appeal. This makes it difficult for the Appeals Chamber to identify all the arguments supporting the appeal.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could kindly ask Your Honour to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: [Previous Translation Continues] ... Emphasise as possible in their oral arguments. The first ground of appeal is entitled "The Drina River incident."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: The first ground of appeal is entitled "The Drina River incident. The appellant alleges that the Trial Chamber committed an error of fact by concluding that the appellant intended that the seven of this incident be killed. Although neither the notice of appeal nor the appeal brief divides this ground into subsections, I have identified three subsidiary grounds among the alleged errors. These are: One, that the appellant was armed on 7 June 1992; two, that when he was at the hotel Vilina Vlas he knew that the seven Muslim men were to be killed and did not try to stop Milan Lukic; and three, that contrarily to the Trial Chamber's findings, he stopped 10 to 15 metres away from the river. The appellant does not appear, however, to address the issue of the impact of the alleged errors on the Trial Chamber's conclusions. I hope that the arguments we hear today will clarify the appellant's position on this issue. The second ground of appeal concerns the appellant's relationship with the paramilitary group led by Milan Lukic. From the written submissions of the appellant, the Appeals Chamber understands that he alleges that the Trial Chamber committed five errors of fact when arriving at the following conclusions: One, the period during which the Lukic group committed crimes; two, that the appellant acted as an informant to the group and did so with full awareness of the -- that the intent of the group was to persecute the local Muslim population of Visegrad; three, that the appellant did not cooperate with the Tribunal; four, that he did not stop all relations with Milan Lukic after the events in question; and five, that he participated in the Musici house search. It appears that under this ground of appeal, the errors and questions are alleged only insofar as they had an impact on sentencing. The third ground of appeal relates to the general requirements of Articles 3 and 5 of the Statute and alleges a series of factual errors in paragraph 46 of the trial judgement; one, that the appellant knew Milan Lukic well; two, that the appellant also knew the other men who were associated with Milan Lukic; three, that the appellant knew that Milan Lukic and his men committed serious crimes; and four, that the appellant, despite that knowledge, was seen together with those men on several occasions during the period relevant to the indictment. In addition, the appellant argues that the Trial Chamber committed errors of fact in paragraphs 48, 51, 54, 57, 58, and 60 of its judgement, by finding that: One, the appellant was standing guard while money and valuables disappeared during the search of Musici; two, non-Serb citizens of Visegrad began disappearing in early April 1992; three, a burnt Muslim woman was denied medical treatment; four, the acts of the appellant were closely related to the armed conflict; and five, the appellant's acts were part of a widespread and systematic attack of which he was aware. The appellant does not appear to address the issue of the impact of these alleged errors on the Trial Chamber's conclusions with respect to this ground of appeal. Again, I hope that in its argument the Defence counsel will clarify this issue. The first ground of appeal relates to the murder of the five Muslims and alleges -- alleges errors in both law and fact. The appellant argues that the Trial Chamber erred in concluding that he shared the intent to kill the seven Muslim men in the Drina River incident. In support of his argument, he states that he was not armed that day and did not point a gun at the seven men in the Vilina Vlas Hotel. He also argues that the intention of Milan Lukic at the time the group was in the hotel was not to kill these seven men but to imprison them. The appellant also points to differences between the testimonies of Witness VG14 and VG32, and argues that their testimonies do not support a finding that the appellant pointed a gun at the seven Muslim men and thereby prevented their escape. The appellant also argues that he was standing 10 to 15 metres behind Milan Lukic and the other two men when the shooting occurred. Some of these arguments overlap with the appellant's submissions under the first ground of appeal. The appellant also raised certain arguments which seemed to be repetitive of arguments raised under the seventh ground of appeal, which concerns a joint criminal enterprise regarding whether there was an agreement among the appellant, Milan Lukic, and the two unknown men, and whether participants in a joint enterprise are equally guilty. Also, under the first ground the appellant alleges an error of law concerning the cumulative convictions. The fifth ground of appeal relates to inhumane acts. The appellant asserts that the Trial Chamber erred by finding, one, that there was an understanding amounting to an agreement by Milan Lukic, the appellant, and two other men to kill the seven Muslim men; and two, that the appellant personally participated in this joint criminal enterprise with the intent to cause VG14 and VG32 serious mental and physical -- or physical suffering. The sixth ground of appeal concerns persecution. First, the appellant submits that the Trial Chamber made an error of law by convicting him for persecutions on the basis of a single incident. Second, the appellant argues that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that he knew that some evil would befall the Koritnik group and that the appellant acted with the intent to discriminate on religious or political grounds. Third, that appellant argues that he did not possess the necessary mens rea for the crime of persecution. The appellant further submits that there was no chain of command between the appellant and the Lukic group and that the discriminatory intent of the members of this group cannot be attributed to the accused without further proof to compensate for this lack of a chain of command. This particular argument, developed at paragraphs 18 and 19 of the Defence additional appeal brief, is not clear and could benefit from clarification by the counsel during the argument. The appellant also raises several arguments under this ground of appeal which overlap with arguments under other grounds, that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that he acted as an informant to the Milan Lukic group, that there is no evidence to support a finding that he intended to kill the seven Muslim men, that there was no agreement between him and other participants to persecute the Muslim population, that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that the appellant was aware of previous illegal acts committed by the Lukic group. The seventh ground of appeal relates to the form of criminal responsibility. The appellant argues that the Trial Chamber committed an error of law, first regarding the requirements necessary required to prove the existence of a joint criminal enterprise. In particular, the appellant submits, and I quote, that "The Trial Chamber fails to explicitly indicate what exact criteria it applies to assess the presence of a joint criminal enterprise." I hope the counsel will clarify this argument and what exact error is alleged. The second alleged error of law regards the conclusion that the participants in a joint criminal enterprise are all equally guilty. The appellant's third sub-ground set out in the additional appeal brief is that the Trial Chamber erred in determining that the appellant shared the intent of the other perpetrators of the joint enterprise. Seven arguments are raised in support of the ground, of which several overlap with arguments asserted elsewhere, especially in the fourth ground of appeal. In his final sub-ground, the appellant argues that the requirements for proving liability as an aider and abettor were not considered but that, in any event, these requirements would not have been satisfied in this case. The eighth ground of appeal relates to sentencing. The appellant argues a general error as to the length of the sentence. Additionally, he raises several alleged errors in relation to the Trial Chamber's consideration of the aggravating factors: One, the method of killing; two, verbal abuse of the victims; three, the trauma suffered by the victims, which is an element of the crime; and four, the discriminatory state of mind, which is also an element of the crime. With regard to mitigating factors, the appellant argues that the Trial Chamber did not consider: One, the appellant's diminished mental responsibility; two, the appellant's remorse; three, the fact that the appellant could not have timely surrendered to the Tribunal because his indictment was confidential; four, the appellant's cooperation with the Prosecution; five, the appellant's relatively minor role in the broader context of the conflict; six, the appellant's lack of involvement in the planning of the offence; and seven, the appellant's conduct while in detention. I would now ask the parties to pay attention to the criteria applicable to errors of fact or law alleged on appeal. As the Appeals Chamber has pointed out on many occasions, the appeal is not an occasion for the parties to re-plead their case. This is not a de novo trial. On appeal, the parties must limit their arguments to the questions which fall within the framework of Article 25 of the Tribunal's Statute. In general, the Appeals Chamber does not hear any arguments but those founded on errors of law which allegedly would invalidate the judgement. Only exceptionally may a party raise a question of general interest for the case law of the Tribunal. As to errors of fact, only those which have caused a miscarriage of justice will be considered. In this case, the great majority of the grounds raised by the appellant deal with alleged errors of fact. As the parties should be well aware, the Appeal Chambers requires the appellant who alleged errors of fact to demonstrate that no reasonable trier of fact could have reached the conclusion being challenged and that the error of fact is of such a gravity as to produce a miscarriage of justice. I would again remind the parties to be very precise and clear in their presentations of the grounds of appeal and their responses and replies. Let me explain our precise schedule for today. As it was set out in our scheduling order of 22 October 2003, the Defence will present its arguments for 2 hours and 30 minutes. We will have a 30-minute break during that presentation. At the end of the Defence presentation, we will have an hour and 30 minutes' break for lunch. After that, the Prosecution will have 2 hours to respond. During that presentation, we will also have a break of 30 minutes. We will then hear the Defence's reply for 30 minutes and then the floor will be given to Mitar Vasiljevic for a brief personal address. I will now give the floor to the Defence -- counsel for the Defence. I call on the counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As lead counsel of the appellant, I will speak in the language of the appellant, the Serbian language, on the B/C/S channel. [Interpretation] The Defence in its appeal has sought to indicate errors of fact which led to a miscarriage of justice in relation to the appellant. In this part of my submissions, I will refer to the facts or, rather, to those errors of fact as the Defence sees them. And my learned colleague, Mr. Knoops, will address the errors of law and present arguments of law. It is my submission that the critical factual errors which have been made and which led to a miscarriage of justice in relation to the appellant were whether there was any intent in his mind to kill the seven men brought to the Vilina Vlas Hotel, whether he knew or could have known in the hotel itself or, rather, before Milan Lukic took them away by car from the hotel. Secondly, a very important issue is whether or not the appellant had a weapon on him on that day, the 7th of June, 1992, because that is an issue that is in dispute yet one of substantive importance. And thirdly, what his role was in the Drina River incident on that day. The other facts that were referred to in the appeal and which indeed are repeated, in view of the paragraphs in which the appeal was written, that is, following the paragraphs and points in the judgement. So there is indeed repetition. But as the President himself indicated today, they have to do with the existence or not of the appellant's link with the Lukic group. Also the periods as to whether he was some sort of an informer, as the Trial Chamber concluded in its judgement, and the Defence will seek, without repeating what has already been said in the appeals brief, to submit its arguments with respect to these very important facts that I mentioned at the beginning. I should just like for the sake of explanation of the general situation that the appellant was in in this period of time, to say a few words with respect to the personality of the accused, and what he was doing in Visegrad in the indictment period. According to what was established during the trial and according to the appellant's submission, the appellant immediately after the Uzice Corps left Visegrad - a period which according to the appeal brief was a rather peaceful and stable period, followed by one that was quite different - the appellant was mobilised and found himself some 10 kilometres or so from Visegrad, in the village of Prelovo, working in the canteen of the Territorial Defence for Visegrad. At that time, he did have a weapon and he was issued with a weapon. This is a period beginning with the end of May 1992, which didn't last long because on the last day of the month of May, sometime around the 1st of June, he refused to carry and distribute food on the front line. He clashed with his superiors in the Territorial Defence command. His rifle was seized from him, and he was sent to a prison, which was set up in the former barracks of the Yugoslav People's Army in Uzamnica, close to Visegrad. This is a fact that according to the Defence the Trial Chamber does accept in its judgement, and it is a fact that the appellant spent several days under such circumstances - according to what he says, three to four days - in prison, from where he was released, in his opinion, because he was given permission to attend the funeral of his cousin. After that he was not sent back to prison but he was also not sent back to his earlier position in Prelovo but was given so-called work assignment to be in charge of the cleaning in town. It is important at this point, in the opinion of the Defence, that during the trial, with reference to these circumstances, his role in street-sweeping, from the first days of June until the 14th of June, 1992, the appellant was seen during his work obligation. He was seen to be in the town of Visegrad. But none of those witnesses who testified to this fact before the Trial Chamber, including several Muslim witnesses, were quoted by the Defence in the appeals brief, quoting the transcripts of their testimony, and none of these witnesses testified that during those two weeks the appellant ever carried a weapon. In the submission of the Defence, this is important precisely because it is asserted that only on the 7th of June, 1992, on the critical day of the Drina River incident, he did carry a weapon. The arguments presented by the Prosecution in their response is correct; namely, that it is possible for him to have had a weapon on that day, whereas he did not have one at any time before or after; and still on the 7th of June, 1992, he could have had a weapon. But it is close to impossible or very, very unlikely that something like that did happen. Since he had given his weapon back to supplies before being sent to prison and did not carry a weapon for more than two weeks, until the 14th of June, 1992, the date when he left Visegrad, it is really extremely unlikely that he would have a weapon on one single occasion, that is, on the 7thof June. In our appeal brief, the Defence analysed precisely that part of the testimony which served as a basis for the finding of the Trial Chamber, that the appellant had a weapon on that critical day; namely, the testimony of VG14 and VG32. However, what is crucial in the opinion of the Defence, when deciding whether the Chamber should accept witness testimony regarding such an essential fact, when testimony is contradictory and the witnesses providing that testimony are people who had suffered mental trauma because of attempts on their own life and murders of their own family, could be motivated perhaps to lay it on the door of the appellant, even though they may not be quite sure that it was something that he had done. It has been established before this Trial Chamber and in the opinion of the Defence it was detrimental to the appellant, because the witnesses who appeared here had only him to blame and he was a very marginal person in Visegrad, as the Defence sought to prove throughout the trial. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. In the submission of the Defence, the fact that these two witnesses, who arrived together from Bikavac, where Milan Lukic, together with two of his soldiers detained them in the Vilina Vlas Hotel, saw the appellant there standing right next to the entrance - and on this point their testimony converges completely - it is impossible that one witness, VG32, pays great attention to the appearance of the appellant, noticing even smaller stains on his shirt and markings and many other details, says that he did not have a weapon at that moment, that he was not moving or saying anything; whereas, the other witness, VG14, referring to the same point in time claims that the appellant carried a weapon and held it in his right hand. During his testimony at trial, the witness said it was an automatic rifle, only to say later when cautioned about his own prior statement, by the Prosecution, that it was a different rifle, not an automatic one; whereas before the Trial Chamber he claimed it was an automatic rifle. Both witnesses asserted that as they were leaving the Vilina Vlas Hotel, the appellant had a rifle. It remains completely unclear how if the appellant did not have a rifle at that time he could procure one precisely for that moment, if he had not been mobilised, if he had not been issued with the weapon, and in the opinion of the Defence this very claim, that he had a rifle at that time, is not accurate and is not true because both the witnesses were aware that the accused could not be found responsible unless he is found to have had a rifle at the time, and it was necessary for them to help somebody get convicted for the crime that was committed against them. And unfortunately for Mitar Vasiljevic, he was the only possibility, the only candidate. Regarding this fact, it is unfortunate that the Trial Chamber committed an error on this point, although this testimony was given many, many years after the incident, and precisely in this case Mitar Vasiljevic demonstrated that such an error was possible because we had more than ten witnesses of the Prosecution who said very emphatically that they used to see the appellant in all sorts of circumstances and situations after the 14th of June, 1992, and they were much more categoric and much more emphatic than the two witnesses who testified that he did have a weapon. But the Trial Chamber did not accept the testimony of the majority of the witnesses in finding that the appellant at that time was in a completely different location from the 14th to the 28th of June, 1992, that is, the Uzice Hospital. In our appeals brief, in addition to this fact concerning the weapon, the Defence pointed out to many other controversies in the testimony of the two witnesses concerned; namely, they either described the events differently, or their testimony was different to the first statements they had given to the investigators of the OTP in the first years after the incidents. Sometimes the differences are minor, such as whether they went towards the Drina River in a file or in a line next to each other or, for instance, who was standing right or left. However, these minor details point to their inability to remember the events exactly in detail and the possibility that they may have been wrong about more important facts, such as whether the appellant had a weapon or not, either unintentionally or intentionally. This seems to be corroborated by the attempt of one of the witnesses to speak during trial about hearing three clicks of a weapon, although he had never mentioned it before. I will not speak about this, because the Trial Chamber did not accept this part of the testimony, even though they had complete trust in the honesty and sincerity of this witness and did not find that this was a fabrication. However, this particular statement, this particular claim was not accepted. However, it still may have led the Trial Chamber to find that the appellant did certainly shoot at the seven people who found their death at the Drina River, despite the fact that none of the two witnesses actually saw it. The Trial Chamber, however, did not accept this and - this is something that I find very important in this case - did not find that the Prosecution had proven beyond a reasonable doubt that the appellant had shot at anyone on that occasion or killed any of these people. It remains contested, of course, and controversial whether he had a weapon and whether intent was present on his part to kill those seven people from the Vilina Vlas Hotel. Speaking about this fact, in the testimony of these witnesses that I mentioned and in the decision of the Trial Chamber itself, it was established that Milan Lukic brought these seven people to the Vilina Vlas Hotel and that in conversations that were confirmed by the witnesses, between Milan Lukic and the person named Susnjar, who was some sort of guard and turnkey in this hotel, he asked for the keys and learned on that occasion that this man, Susnjar, had already released some of the people who had been detained there, with the explanation that he was not able to keep them there any longer because Milan Lukic had not been coming there for several days and he had nothing to feed them with, so he released them. This fact, in the submission of the Defence, is very important because it shows that the appellant, who found himself there by chance and found what that was all about and learnt that the people who had been detained there previously were released and that those seven people had been brought there and detained -- the appellant, as was found by the Trial Chamber, must have brought them there with the intent to detain them and to keep them and use them for some sort of exchange that were frequent at that time between Serbs and Muslims. The fact that he insisted on the keys so much and that he wanted to detain, to lock up these people, and the fact that not a single word was said about possible execution, as well as the fact that since he was not able to keep them there, he said they were going back, is tale-telling. Even those two witnesses who were heard by the Trial Chamber did not suspect that something else would occur, and the soldier who was part of the escort also testified. We know that there was another prison in Uzamnica on the other side of Visegrad, and we know that none of the witnesses, VG14 and 32 included, or the appellant, suspected that what happened would happen; namely, that after crossing 2 or 3 kilometres and reaching the bank of the Drina River, Milan Lukic would order these people to go towards the Drina, where within a few minutes a tragedy would occur, wherein these people would be executed. As to the role of the appellant, the Trial Chamber proceeded on the assumption that the appellant had the intent and the wish to have these people executed and that was why the reason -- that was the reason why he accompanied those seven people, whose arrest he had not previously known about, and that he somehow participated in this. The Defence tried, both during the trial and in its appeals brief to present its arguments to the contrary, both regarding knowledge that these people would be killed and the point when it actually happened on the bank of the Drina River, that Milan Lukic would shoot these people dead when he was unable to do anything about it. And the last point is: What could the appellant have done to help those three people? It is the submission of the Defence that it is very important to point out that no role or assistance of the appellant was needed by these three, either at that moment or otherwise, because as it has been established beyond any doubt, if these three could have on the Bikavac hill, several hours before this, searching houses they arrested not these seven but many more people, according to the testimony, at least twice as many people -- if in doing so they didn't need the assistance of anyone - and there was a possibility for the attack to be resisted, because this was an entire settlement that was in question, and they could have put up resistance - if in that -- on that occasion they hadn't needed any aid, they needed aid still less at this point in time, when they were bringing them back from the Vilina Vlas Hotel. Regrettably the Trial Chamber did not accept the testimony of the appellant about this, nor his assertion that he could do nothing, and that when he saw what was about to happen he never approached the site of the crime or the banks of the Drina, that he remained among the trees that was some distance away from the river bank. This was not accepted by the Trial Chamber, and in the submission of the Defence it is an error of fact which is of extreme importance and which leads to a miscarriage of justice in this case, in relation to the appellant. In the submission of the Defence, the Trial Chamber Judges completely neglected the testimony of a very important witness, though they did trust him and they did not challenge his testimony. But in the opinion of the Defence, it was wrongly interpreted to the detriment of the appellant, rather than in his favour. In my opinion, an exhaustive explanation is given of this point in the appeals brief, and I shall now just highlight a few of the most important points which I consider to be important for this Chamber and your ruling today. This witness, unlike two other eyewitnesses, apart from being Muslim, was in no way motivated to testify prejudicially because though he recognised two among the victims, in the opinion of the Defence, he testified truthfully of what he saw and what he could have seen from the other bank of the Drina River through his binoculars. It is very important to point out that he was very familiar with Mitar Vasiljevic personally. He knew him extremely well. He knew him and recognised him in other situations as well. And this is important because during his testimony about what had happened, he did not see Mitar Vasiljevic, that is, the appellant, on the Drina river bank. Even in his statement for the investigators, given a year prior to this trial, he drew a sketch of what he had seen, and this is Defence Exhibit D1, which I would kindly ask this Chamber to pay special attention to, which he recognised as his and as being authentic, and he drew the positions of the seven unarmed men along the Drina, among whom he recognised two of -- who were his friends, and he recognised and identified them accurately. And after that, he marked the position of three soldiers who were standing behind and who shot at these seven, which he saw and heard. He did not see a fourth man in that position, that is, the appellant in this case. It is true that at the hearing itself, during his testimony, and also when examined by the Prosecution, he said that he saw a group stop, two vehicles, and seven civilians walking in front, and three or four soldiers going behind them; that is, a total of 10 or 11 persons. In view of the fact that in his written statement, which he recognised, he was talking about three plus seven, that is a total of ten persons, when he spoke to the investigator. When I asked him about it, he said that this fourth or eleventh person was one that he didn't see very well and that he wasn't even sure that he -- that it existed, that he thought he saw 10 or 11 or 3 or 4 when approaching the river but not at the river itself and that probably if such a fourth or eleventh person did exist, this person was left behind among the trees, and that is why he didn't see him. It is a well-founded assumption of the Defence that this fourth man, who could not be seen and who was among the trees is the appellant, and we do so -- we believe so for the following reasons: On the one hand, the witness himself said that he knew the appellant very well and that in view of the fact that among the seven he was able to recognise two of his acquaintances, he would have certainly recognised among three soldiers the appellant if he had been there, especially as with regard to one of the three he said that he even noticed that he had rather light-coloured hair and that on that basis he later concluded that it was Milan Lukic, who had such hair. And another important fact, which this witness noticed, and that is that all three were wearing uniforms of the same colour. He claimed that he saw that as being a dark colour, a black -- or rather, black. Other witnesses about this uniform describe it as being a blue camouflage uniform that was worn by members of the police. So in any case, it was certainly a dark uniform, and it is beyond dispute, even according to the statements of the witnesses, the appellant on that occasion was wearing a light-coloured, old so-called SMB olive-green/grey uniform on him, which was quite different from that worn by the others. This, in the opinion of the Defence, is a very important fact, and it indicates that the appellant was not among those standing behind the victims, that is, Milan Lukic and his two soldiers, and that he did not participate in shooting these men, and that these three who did shoot and the way in which they shot led to two survivors. This witness confirmed what the appellant was saying, and I must recall, as this was referred to in the closing statement of the Prosecution, that the appellant adjusted his defence to the statement of this witness, which is not correct, because when the appellant first made his statement to the Prosecution, it was on the 16th and 17th of November, 2000, when he described the situation in the same manner, the situation on the Drina River, and Witness VG79 was heard and found by the Prosecution for the first time and interviewed in 2001 and the appellant was not aware of his statement at the time. So I believe that these facts are of great importance indeed and that the Trial Chamber erred in its findings with regard to these facts. And this is of key importance for the Drina River incident for which Mitar Vasiljevic was found guilty. These facts are, therefore, very important, because all other facts that are in dispute, that is, those referred to by the President of the Tribunal and discussed in the appeal brief relations with Lukic, relations between Lukic and this group, and all the other matters, whether he was or not some sort of an informer, this may have an impact on something else, on the sentencing if found guilty for this Drina River incident, that is, the killing on the Drina River which led to a guilty sentence cumulatively for several crimes, though it is a single event that is in question. And it is our submission that it is essential to establish, first of all, whether the appellant was armed, whether he wanted the death of these people, and whether he was a participant in any way in their execution, which I think is more important than all the others, which, of course, I will refer to but much less so, as they were addressed in detail in the appeal briefs. Naturally, taking into account everything that was done at the time, the Trial Chamber focussed in particular, using as the main argument for the intent of the appellant to participate in this killing, the Trial Chamber stated that the appellant was aware that at that time Milan Lukic and his group had committed a series of terrible crimes and that this was the grounds on which they found that he knew and should have known that such a thing would happen on the Drina river bank. In the appeal brief, the Defence denied this fact and challenged it, indicating specific parts of the transcript regarding the statements of the accused, saying that the opposite was true, that is, the crimes of Milan Lukic which may have been known to the accused occurred later and that he learnt about them much later and that he personally was not aware of any crime committed by Milan Lukic before the 7th or June, nor could he have known about it. I think this is corroborated to some extent by the indictment of the Prosecution in this case. In the indictment itself, the first specific incident that Milan Lukic is charged with was the 7th of June, that is, the Drina River incident. And then come the following events, the factory, the Pionirska Street on the 14th of June and then the other incidents. So if it is true, as claimed by the Prosecution, that Milan Lukic, before the 7th of June, had committed some grave crimes that they have knowledge about, in the opinion of the Defence they would have been part of the indictment and included in the indictment as specific incidents. However, this is lacking. Whereas, the accused -- or rather, the appellant is charged with those very crimes. On the other hand, as I said at the very beginning, the appellant in those days was mobilised; that is, he was in the Territorial Defence in Prelovo, and it is true that he frequently came home to spend the night because he wasn't a soldier in the strict sense of the word but he was working in supplies and in cooking in the canteen, because he was by profession a waiter anyway, so he was able to notice certain things. And on one occasion, which was referred to at some length in the judgement - and I will refer to it too - the village of Musici, when from Prelovo, as he was wont, as he found a means of transport to spend the night at home, on one of those last days in May he was driven by Milan Lukic himself who stopped in Musici on that occasion. And the Trial Chamber analysed that event and devoted quite considerable attention to it when discussing the relationship between Milan Lukic and the appellant. With respect to that incident, which was not specifically part of the indictment but which is of significance in this opinion of the Trial Chamber, because it is claimed that on that occasion the appellant was standing guard while Milan Lukic was searching a house in Musici and that some valuables disappeared from some houses on that occasion. Very briefly, I should like to comment on this because I think it was elaborated in detail in the appeals brief. I would say that this was a period that preceded his arrest, a period when he was part of the Territorial Defence and when he himself said that on that occasion he was travelling with a weapon from Prelovo to his home, that he was armed, and that a group of three vehicles arrived, one -- in one of which Milan Lukic was, and that they took him in the direction of Visegrad, and that 2 or 3 kilometres later, passing through the village of Musici on that route, the vehicle was stopped and Milan Lukic entered the house. I think that the explanation and testimony of the appellant is accurate and trustworthy. He showed how embarrassed he felt because Milan Lukic went into a house on that occasion, that is, the house of VG55's father, asking whether they had weapons, because it was asserted that the police had been shot at from that house. The role of the appellant in this event, who didn't even wish to enter the house - he stood at the open door - was to show that he knew these people, that they were good people, and that there was no reason for anyone to have any suspicions about them, including Milan Lukic. Nothing happened on that occasion. The witnesses who testified about this, VG55 and 79, said that there was no mistreatment or anything like that, that there was a discussion of weapons; and that Milan Lukic asked the people from the other houses to come out, for him to tell them that, that the other people did come, that he gave them a speech, and after that they left. It is true that after that, according to the testimony of these witnesses, that in these houses, not the house in front of which the appellant was standing and into which Milan Lukic went, that from these other houses that the other soldiers of Milan Lukic went into, that some valuables disappeared, some money and other things, but that truly cannot have anything to do with the appellant, who didn't even know about it and heard about it for the first time here in court, when it was testified about. But he was never again in the company of these people and he explained why on that night he was in Milan Lukic's vehicle. However, that event, in the submission of the Defence, is very important precisely for another reason, because of another thing that we heard testimony about. Those witnesses, VG55 -- in fact both sons of the man whose house was searched and who came here to testify, were members of the reserve force of the police for a while before the war began. Both were Muslims. The appellant knew this and testified to this, and he testified precisely about the fact that he had certain misgivings that Milan Lukic might find weapons in their houses because reserve policemen did keep weapons at home. On that occasion, he wanted the whole thing to end as soon as possible and to get to Visegrad as soon as possible, and he was trying to stop Milan Lukic and to hurry him on, and in doing so he did not mention this fact to Milan Lukic. This is also important because of another thing. Although the Trial Chamber did not find that by providing any information the appellant helped Milan Lukic in any way and did not charge him with it, it -- it still says in the judgement "some kind of informant" and this finding is based on one fact alone, namely that one of these witnesses asked by Milan Lukic said that a house on the Drina River belonged to Muslims. In fact, the appellant said that one of these houses belonged to Muslims. And the Defence agrees, that Milan Lukic did ask this question and the appellant said that it belonged to Muslims. But it has no importance. This house is still standing. A group of witnesses identified this whole location, this whole area, and that is referred to in Exhibit P18. However, this whole incident is made up, according to the appellant, because he says he never said such a thing. The house belonged to a man named Kosoric and there was no reason for this. And to find that somebody was an informant for a criminal group based on such flimsy ground, is very important in the submission of the Defence. At the same time, the appellant had opportunity to become an informant and did not do so, nor did he provide any important information. On the other hand, Milan Lukic's group had no need to use him as an informant, because they had informants of their own. For a couple of years before the war began, Milan Lukic was a resident of Visegrad himself. He knew the area quite well, and he knew people in Visegrad. And even the people he had brought from Obrenovac were locals -- were originally from Visegrad. In view of the testimony of witnesses who say that they wore police uniforms and were stationed in police quarters, it seems unlikely to me that he required any assistance, in terms of information regarding the residents of Visegrad. The only evidence underlying this finding is precisely this one, that happened on the bank of the Drina and the stopping of the car. I am pointing out this fact and important contradictions between the testimony of two witnesses, in light of the fact that the appellant did not utter a single word, either at the Vilina Vlas Hotel or during the whole incident, which lasted for over ten minutes. Therefore, his relationship with the Lukic group, in light of this event in Musici and the claim that he was some sort of informant with full knowledge, as it is asserted, is an error, is an erroneous finding of the Trial Chamber, in the submission of the Defence, and we corroborate our submission with the arguments I have just stated, testimony of his utterances at that house and the incident in Musici and the fact that he knew that those people were reserve policemen, which he kept to himself, is much more important in the submission of the Defence, because it shows he was not willing to assist Milan Lukic. There are other several things that the Trial Chamber found important in finding whether he indeed had a relationship with the Lukic group. The Trial Chamber did not accept the claim of the Prosecution that the appellant was a member of that group, and we believe this is really Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. important. However, the finding of the Trial Chamber, with respect to the Drina River incident, contributed largely to his conviction and his very harsh sentence. In the opinion of the Defence, the main reason and the main argument against his being an informant is the incident in Musici, because what he is charged with is that he was seen on several occasions in the company of Milan Lukic. In the appeals brief, the Defence stated that this was not accurate because in reality there were only two occasions; namely, the Musici incident and the Drina River incident. There was no other contact, no other meeting between the appellant and Milan Lukic throughout that period. And the whole event should not have been treated in this way and interpreted as his being in the company of Milan Lukic on several occasions. Another issue on which -- to which I believe the Trial Chamber attributed great importance is whether the appellant could have done anything to prevent Milan Lukic from committing that crime on the 7th of June, 1992 on the Drina River. Could he have dissuaded him? During examination of Witnesses VG14 and VG32, the Defence asked them directly to give their assessment of what happened on the bank of the Drina River and to describe their experience and to say whether any of those present could have exerted any influence on Milan Lukic or prevented what happened. Both witnesses, VG14 and VG32, said without thinking and certainly without taking into account whether it could be of assistance to the appellant, said as one that such a person did not exist. In our appeals brief, we quoted that from the transcript of the testimony of these two witnesses. In its judgement, the Trial Chamber cited that despite this statement of those witnesses, the appellant could have done something, and here they refer to the fact that during the incident in Musici he intervened successfully. The Trial Chamber did not provide any clearer explanation as to what they found the appellant to have done that was of such great importance in Musici, especially in light of the fact that we know of another situation, which I described, in a completely different atmosphere, where there was no arrest going on, no attempt of murder, when the only issue was whether a house needed to be searched or not. And the Trial Chamber accepted it seems that the appellant did say to Milan Lukic that the people who lived in that house were good and they -- their house needed not to be searched, but it does not mean that he could have dissuaded Milan Lukic from detaining those people or keeping them as hostages. So the Musici event does not demonstrate that the appellant could have intervened in the other incident, and the testimony of the two witnesses we heard corroborates this. What remains to be established is whether the appellant uttered anything at the moment of the shooting, whether any of the victims was asking for something and whether the appellant said anything at that moment. Witness testimony differs on this point. Some say that victims were pleading and that the appellant did say something; another witness says that Mitar Vasiljevic did not say anything. And Meho Dzavic stated that Mitar Vasiljevic said he did not know the man. And another witness says that immediately after the utterances of Meho Dzavic, shooting occurred. And from the position where we believe the appellant was, he could not have said anything. As for Article 3.5, about the perfect awareness of the appellant of the crimes, there is one finding which I believe is detrimental to the appellant, and it had nothing to do with the criminal activity of Milan Lukic and his group; namely, the relationship between the families of Vasiljevic and Lukic, which dates back to 100 years ago. A lot has been said before the Trial Chamber about the best-man relationship, which considerably damaged the case of the appellant. This relationship is not a personal one between the two men; it is a relationship between families. And I emphasise this because it concerns not the family of Mitar Vasiljevic, his wife, and children, and the family of Milan Lukic, but about a dozen families that have continued this relationship for a long time through their marriages, baptisms, ceremonies, et cetera. So there was no direct best-man relationship between the two men. It was a relationship between the two families. And I believe the Trial Chamber did not pay enough attention to this, because it found that at that time they had a close relationship and that this somehow affected the knowledge he could have had about the activities of Milan Lukic. Thirty years before that, when Milan Lukic set up his family, Mitar Vasiljevic was a child, and then he went to Belgrade and Switzerland and came back to Visegrad just before the war. So there was no direct relationship between them. There was only acquaintance, which to his great misfortune led him to ask for a lift on that occasion on the road, on that unfortunate day, and which he explained when speaking about that time near the Vilina Vlas Hotel, when Milan Lukic had already brought that group of people. What he said about the fact that Milan Lukic had not been in that hotel for many days shows that Mitar Vasiljevic found himself there on that day by chance. And if what Susnjar says is correct, that the Lukic group had not visited for several days and that was the reason why he released some prisoners, then Mitar Vasiljevic says accurately that he could not have known that they would show up precisely on that day. There is another point; namely, the appellant's own testimony before the Trial Chamber and his statements to the Prosecution, which were not taken into account either as a mitigating circumstance and -- or as cooperation with the Prosecution. On the contrary, the Prosecution attempted to place it in a quite different context; namely, that whatever he testified from direct knowledge or from hearsay, referring to events after the 7th of June about Milan Lukic and the people who kept company with him, was interpreted by the Prosecution as his membership in that group. It was even argued that Defence witnesses did not refer to such similar knowledge, that among the names shown to them they only recognised Sredoje Lukic, that is, one of the also accused here, and that they didn't testify about that. In the submission of the Defence - and it is true that those witnesses did not confirm that, most probably because they were personally afraid of talking about people who were still alive and at large somewhere in the territories of the former Yugoslavia, and that is why those witnesses were not willing to testify about that, and they mostly said that they didn't remember or didn't know those people. The appellant, in the submission of the Defence, had the courage and the wish to act in an opposite manner, and he provided a great deal of information about many of those people in his testimony, regardless of the fact that his family is still living there and they are at considerable risk, and the Defence really regrets not only that this was not accepted as being cooperation or in mitigation of his acts but in fact was even used against him to some extent. I wouldn't specifically refer to VGD3 and VGD4's identification, because of the public nature of this hearing, but this can be found in the transcript and in the response, in the confidential version of the response to the Prosecution brief, which was left out from the public version, and I think that this is very important for disproving what is stated in the position of the Prosecution and partially also in the Trial Chamber findings, that there was no real cooperation by the appellant. I have sought to refer to the most important grounds of appeal contained in the appeal brief, and after hearing the Prosecution's submissions, I may have some additional remarks to make. But for the present, that would be my -- those would be my submissions regarding errors of fact. utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. By the way, my submissions and authorities are available in written form with some additions, so I could present them to your Court if you wish it so. In addition to Mr. Domazet's pleadings, the Defence intends to further elaborate on five major legal issues pertaining to this case, which invalidate the Trial Chamber's decision due to several errors of law, which are for some part intertwined with errors of fact, amounting to a miscarriage of justice as no reasonable trier of fact could have reached these conclusions. I will also point on which way these errors seriously impacted on the Trial Chamber conclusions. In my submissions, I will first address the error of law, both with respect to actus reus and mens rea with regard to the joint criminal enterprise, and I will address also the remark of Your Honours with respect to the stipulation as to what exactly were the errors of law in view of the Defence. Secondly, I will address the errors of law with regard to the crime of persecution and their impacts on the Trial Chamber conclusions. My further -- my third chapter deals with the crime of murder, specifically appeal grounds number 4. Fourth, I will discuss the existence of an error of law with regard to the aggravating factors, as mentioned in the appeal grounds number 8. Fifthly and lastly, my last chapter of the submissions is dedicated to the fact -- fact which recently emerged, and the Defence will point out to the Appeals Chamber a potential new sentencing consideration, namely the recent conviction of Mr. Lukic by a Belgrade district criminal court on 29 September 2003 for similar acts as those which took place on the 7th June 1992 and which facts could be taken into consideration by the Appeals Chamber pursuant Rule 94, which provides that a Trial Chamber shall not require proof of facts of common knowledge, which shall take judicial notice thereof. In conjunction with Rule 170, the Appeals Chamber is, in view of the Defence, empowered to take notice of this fact, to which I return later. The aforementioned errors of law, Your Honours, relate to several errors of substantive law and are of such nature that they should in itself or in conjunction with the errors of law and fact lead to a reversal of the Trial Chamber judgement. Your Honours, these submissions will start with addressing several errors of law as to the concept of joint criminal enterprise and their impact on the Trial Chamber's conclusions. First of all, before assessing the requisite mens rea as to this concept, the requisite actus reus as to this doctrine is examined from the perspective of error of law in this particular case. An important argument to revise the decision taken by the Trial Chamber as to the latter criterion may be found in a recent judgement of Trial Chamber II, in which case several similarities arise with respect to the position of the appellant. In its judgement of October 17 of this year, the ICTY Trial Chamber II and Prosecutor versus Simic et al. Contemplated in the paragraphs 998 and 999 with respect to the accused Miroslav Tadic the following: While there was evidence in this case, according to the Chamber, that he was present at the detention facilities and had knowledge of their existence and conditions and visited these sites, this could not lead to the conclusion that his actions had a substantial effect on the perpetration of the offence of unlawful arrest and detention and, accordingly, to several other actions. The Trial Chamber was in that case not beyond reasonable doubt satisfied that that accused shared the discriminatory intent of the joint criminal enterprise to persecute non-Serb civilians through their unlawful arrest and detention, his continued participation in conducting exchanges and transferring detainees, his attendance at meetings of the Crisis Staff and with some of the other direct participants in the joint criminal enterprise in Belgrade, where the role of the paramilitaries were discussed. And despite the fact that the Trial Chamber ruled that Mr. Tadic had knowledge of the discriminatory intent of the joint criminal enterprise, it nevertheless acquitted him due to the fact that he was not in a position with power to prevent the work of the joint criminal enterprise and the corresponding criminal activity. Mr. President, Your Honours, from this recent decision, three major legal arguments may be deduced which are equally applicable to the present case of the appellant: First, equally to Mr. Tadic in the Simic case, no evidence exists as to the extent that Mr. Vasiljevic was contacted to make any decisions on the arrest or detention of non-Serbs. Furthermore, no conclusive facts exist which justify the conclusion that it was established beyond reasonable doubt, that the appellant shared the discriminatory intent of the joint criminal enterprise to persecute non-Serb civilians through - and I quote the Trial Chamber's decision in the Simic case - "a continued participation in conducting exchanges and transferring detainees, his attendance at meetings," et cetera. Notably, Mr. President, this accused, Mr. Tadic, was accused of being implicated in a joint criminal enterprise through a continued participation. Therefore, in contrast to the appellant, the actions of that accused, according to said judgement, were of a more permanent. Nature, as the conviction of the appellant is, however, merely based on one particular and exceptional situation - I will return to this argument later - during which the appellant was present, the judgement of the Trial Chamber cannot be upheld. Second, the Trial Chamber held that despite of the knowledge of this discriminatory intent towards non-Serbs and knowledge of said intent of the joint criminal enterprise in the Simic case, "the actions or missions of that particular accused, Tadic, could not be considered to have had a substantial effect on the perpetration of the offence." Your Honours, the element of a substantial effect is clearly absent in the case of the appellant. At least, no conclusive facts arise which justify the conclusion that his, Mr. Vasiljevic's, actions or omissions have had such an effect on the perpetration of the crimes committed at the Drina River on the 7th of June. Your Honours, I especially point you to paragraph 252 of the judgement, where it is said - I quote - "There is no basis in the evidence for finding beyond reasonable doubt what specific crimes were committed by Milan Lukic group which resulted from the assistance given by the accused or that the accused was sufficiently aware of the circumstances in which Milan Lukic group would use the information he gave them so as to constitute him as an aider and abettor of the crimes which they committed." Your Honours, this conclusion of the Trial Chamber itself indeed reviewed the acceptance of the elements of substantial effect and should be led to a review of that acceptance. Reference may be made to the case of Prosecutor versus Kvocka, in which the Trial Chamber indeed held that the degree of participation required must be significant; that is to say, it must make the enterprise efficient or effective. It is said that, in that case, "The level of participation attributed to the accused and whether the participation is deemed significant will depend on a variety of factors, including the size of the enterprise, the functions performed, the position of the accused, the amount of time spent participating after acquiring knowledge of the criminality of the system, efforts made to prevent activity or to impede the efficient functioning of the system," et cetera. As these criterion clearly are not met with respect to the appellant, the appeal should be granted already based on --

Also to this element, I return later. Mr. Vasiljevic himself witnessed on October 26, 2001, before the Trial Chamber, and there he stressed that he was not in a position to stop Mr. Lukic and his men from committing their crimes. His witness statement of that date reveals very interesting and important elements. He is questioned at that time by Mr. Groome of the Prosecutor. And there Mr. Vasiljevic inter alia emphasises - I quote - Mr. Groome asked, "What did you do?" Mr. Vasiljevic: "I begged him. I said, 'Milan, please don't. These people haven't done any harm to you. Leave them alone.' But it was to no avail. He couldn't be persuaded. He was so angry. And I was trying to reason with him, to explain to him that I had known Meho for years," et cetera. Mr. President, given these statements, it was clear that the appellant was not in a position to influence the decision made by Milan Lukic and that group, and this conclusion is supported by the only two witnesses in this tragic incident, VG32 and VG14. Their statements are cited by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 107, saying that the impression was that nobody around Milan Lukic could have prevented him from acting. In conclusion, based on the findings of the Trial Chamber in Prosecutor versus Simic, it is justified to say that no reasonable Tribunal could have held the appellant criminally liable, based on the concept of joint criminal enterprise, due to presence at the crime scene, even if one were to accept that the appellant had a weapon - which is refuted already by the pleadings of Mr. Domazet. I will return for the specific element of presence at the crime scene in another section of my submissions. But more arguments arise which merit this specific conclusion that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have reached the conclusion that the appellant participated in a joint criminal enterprise. From the case law of the ICTY, with respect to this form of individual criminal responsibility, several important criteria emerge. And I will examine them shortly, especially their impact on the Trial Chamber's conclusions in this case. An individual who himself did not physically commit these crimes Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. may nonetheless be held criminally responsible for an act which went beyond the agreed object of that crime. The main requirement of joint criminal enterprise is that the intent is shared with the principal offender, thus embracing actions perpetrated by collectivity of persons in furtherance of a common criminal design. In the case of the appellant, according to the Trial Chamber, this shared or common intent was deemed to be present on the part of the appellant. Accordingly, as stated by the Prosecution in paragraph 8.5 of its respondent's brief, it found the first category of joint criminal enterprise applicable, as it held that the accused was present at the time of the commission of the crime with knowledge that the crime is to be or is being committed, by intentionally assisting or encouraging another participant in this joint criminal enterprise. However, the Trial Chamber unjustly accepted and applied the requisite criteria for the first category of joint criminal enterprise. In the Tadic appeals judgement, also referred to in the Simic case, the Appeals Chamber held that for joint criminal enterprise to be constituted, the following elements need to be fulfilled: A polarity of persons, a common plan, a participation of the accused in the common plan, a shared intent between all the participants. And the intent on part of the accused that the result is affected. In the case of persecution, there is an additional element which needs to be fulfilled; namely, that all participants in the common plan had a discriminatory intent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I see it. Sorry. Your Honours, for this subject, reference is made to paragraphs 63 of the judgement, where the Trial Chamber accepts that the extended form of joint criminal enterprise is not relied on and that only the first and second category should be considered. This was also the position taken by the Prosecution in the paragraphs 8.5, 8.9, and 8.14 of its respondent's brief. Now, this observation is quite important for this appeal. Let us face now the element of common purpose and its impact on the Trial Chamber observations, as endorsed by the Tadic Appeals Chamber judgement, in which judgement this doctrine was developed in the paragraphs 185, 192. The first category of this doctrine was identified as follows: In cases of co-perpetration, all participants in the common design must possess the same criminal intent to commit a crime and one or more of them actually should perpetrate the crime with intent. However, in the case of the appellant, no facts arise according to which a reasonable Tribunal could conclude that the appellant was involved in a common design to pursue one course of conduct, in terms of this first category. In paragraph 204 of the Tadic appeals judgement, an example is mentioned; namely, the situation of a common shared intention on part of a group to forcibly remove members of one ethnicity from their town with the consequence that, in the course of doing so, one of the victims is shot and killed. In such a situation, murder or another crime may nevertheless be foreseeable as a result of the removal. In the case of the appellant, however, the facts do not indicate the presence of such a shared common intention, as envisioned by the first category regarding the appellant. To the contrary; the following paragraphs of the Trial Chamber judgement make the opposite plausible. In paragraph 75 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber holds that it - I quote - "is not satisfied that the association" -- with -- the alleged association of Mr. Lukic -- "is a sufficient basis by itself for any finding that the accused shared the general homicidal intentions of their group." Your Honours, this observation by the Trial Chamber is repeated in two other paragraphs, namely 79 and 95. So on three different locations in the judgement, the Trial Chamber accepts that the accused -- the appellant did not share the general homicidal intentions of the group of Milan Lukic. Paragraph 252, already mentioned. And Your Honours are right that it's being referred to in the context of another incident, but the Defence holds that the observations of the Trial Chamber have also some merit with respect to the Drina River incident. Paragraph 305: The non-taking part of the appellant in the planning of the execution of the five Muslim men and the element of becoming only involved in view of the Trial Chamber at the time when these men were brought to the hotel a short time before they were killed. This seems to the Defence a circumstance which also refutes the alleged implication with respect to singling out of these men and the alleged involvement of the accused with respect to singling out. I will return to this topic later. In conclusion, based on the very findings of the Trial Chamber itself, it unjustly accepted liability based on the first category of joint criminal enterprise, in terms of attribution of the perpetration of crimes by a collectivity of persons, in furtherance of a common criminal design, to the appellant. In the event the Appeals Chamber would negate the first category of joint criminal enterprise and judge upon the third category, the Defence refers to the decisions of the Trial Chamber in Prosecutor Krnojelac, where it held that it is not allowed to charge someone with the basic form of joint criminal enterprise and consequently outside the scope of the indictment or amended indictment hold the accused responsible based upon the extended form thereof. Therefore, the Defence prays that the Appeals Chamber primarily will only look into the first category of joint criminal enterprise. However, alternatively, in the event the Appeals Chamber were to look also to the third category, the Defence points your Chamber to the decision on the form of the further amended indictment and Prosecution application to amend in Prosecutor versus Brdjanin and Talic, in which decision further details were provided as to determining the element of foreseeability as to the third category. It may be concluded that foreseeability, as envisioned by the jurisprudence of the ICTY, is far from conclusively reached in this case and does not follow from the facts of the case. In this context, the question arises whether the accused's mere presence at the Drina River can constitute the alleged participation to the joint criminal enterprise or, alternatively, can determine the charge of aiding and abetting. I will briefly assess this element and its impact on the Trial Chamber observations. Your Honours, in the Tadic opinion and judgement of 7 May 1997, the Trial Chamber contemplated, in paragraph 689, that presence alone is not sufficient if it is an ignorant or unwilling presence. However, if the presence can be shown to be knowing and communatively [sic] to have a direct and substantial effect on the commission of the illegal act, it could lead to criminal culpability. Therefore, mere presence alone cannot amount to criminal liability, also not in the realm of joint criminal enterprise, unless this presence would have an encouraging effect or support. This notion follows also from paragraph 690 of said Tadic judgement and also from the Furundzija trial judgement where the Trial Chamber stated that presence, "when combined with authority, can constitute assistance in the form of moral support; that is, the actus reus of the offence." Your Honours, such a combination with authority may certainly not be derived from the facts of this case. To the contrary, the Trial Chamber accepted that the appellant was not even part of the paramilitary group of Milan Lukic - see paragraph 95 of the judgement, in which it is also held that there is no basis for any finding, according to the Trial Chamber, that the accused shared the general homicidal intentions of the group - repeated, as I mentioned, in paragraphs 75 and 79. The Furundzija decision is for this case also relevant with respect to another argument. The supporter must be of a certain status for this, to constitute any assistance when present at the crime scene, must therefore have a certain status to be sufficient for criminal responsibility. This argument was reinforced by the Aleksovski Trial Chamber judgement, where the Trial Chamber similarly held that it should be ascertained whether presence had a significant effect on the perpetration of the crime and that only presence, when coupled with a position of authority occupied by the accused, can establish criminal liability under Article 7, Section 1 of the Statute. The Foca trial judgement, Your Honours, confirmed this requisite element, stating that - I quote - "Presence alone at the scene of the crime is not conclusive of aiding and abetting, unless it is shown to have a significant legitimising effect on the principal." And as noticed, such position of authority was not occupied by the appellant, even not in view of the Trial Chamber itself. Your Honours, in this context, a final and decisive argument arises. In paragraph 95, the Trial Chamber seems to infer the alleged participation of the appellant from the fact that he had some association with the Lukic group, and then it says, "In that he willingly acted has an informant to that group." Now, this observation is in clear contravention to paragraph 302 of the judgement, where the Trial Chamber contemplates that the accused was not a commander, his crimes were geographically very limited, and - and that's the bottom line, quote - "There is no evidence that his acts encouraged other offenders other than as found in relation to the Drina River incident." Mr. President, this implies that the alleged participation of the appellant cannot be found upon prior alleged contacts between the appellant, on the one hand, and said group, on the other hand, so that the weighing of the evidence is and should solely be confined to the date of 7 June 1992. And may I point you to paragraph 75 of the judgement, saying that the accused was a ready source of local information for that group about the location of Muslims in the area. This argument of the Trial Chamber, apparently launched to establish alleged participation in a joint criminal enterprise, is also not consistent with the mentioned paragraph, 302 of the judgement. And this inconsistency may be seen as an error of law or fact. Consequently, in conjunction with the mentioned arguments, the absence of encouraging acts prior to 7 June 1992 on the part of the appellant, refutes, therefore, the alleged participation which the Trial Chamber found on the elements in paragraph 75. Now, this section of the submissions, the assessment of participation of joint criminal enterprise, arrives at this conclusion: The Defence holds that the Trial Chamber erred in law, intertwined with factual errors, by accepting individual criminal responsibility of the appellant, based on the concept of joint criminal enterprise, and seeks thus for an acquittal by your Appeals Chamber due to five observations, which are justified based upon my examination, observations which seriously impact the validity of the Trial Chamber observations. First, the absence of a permanent situation of alleged participation. I refer to inter alia the Simic decision. Second, the absence of evidence beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant shared the discriminatory intent of the joint criminal enterprise, as well as the absence of sharing a common intention; and also, alternatively - it only relates to the third category - the absence of foreseeability. Three, the absence of a direct, substantial, and significant effect on the perpetration of the charged crimes, persecution of murder, on the part of the appellant. Four, the absence of a position with power to prevent the work of the joint criminal enterprise and corresponding criminal activity, an element derived from permanent case law of the ICTY. Fifth, the absence of the requisite authority or status on the part of the appellant, in order to elevate mere presence at the crime scene into the level of individual criminal responsibility, as enshrined by Article 7, Section (1) of the Statute. Accordingly, the actus reus element required for joint criminal enterprise, related to the charged two offences, is not fulfilled and no reasonable Tribunal could have reached another conclusion, so that the appellant should be acquitted. Now, these submissions arrive at the element of mens rea required for proof of participation in a joint criminal enterprise and I will assess their -- its impact on the Trial Chamber observations. In view of the Defence, Your Honours, this mens rea element should be distinguished from the special intent which is conditional for persecution. Only after the former mens rea in relation to joint criminal enterprise is proven, the issue of special intent required for persecution comes into view. Therefore, in the event your Chamber would accept that either the Trial Chamber erred in law or proof as to the former mens rea could not have been reached by any reasonable Court, it is no longer necessary to legally assess the issue of special intent as to persecution. In the event the Trial Chamber judgement should be read as referring indeed to the first category of joint criminal enterprise, it needs -- it needs to be proven that all members of that enterprise possess the same criminal intention. This is also the assumption of the Prosecutor, as envision by its respondent's brief, in paragraph 88 of its brief it is submitted that "this is a straightforward incident of that category of cases," the first category. Now, close reading of the Trial Chamber judgement learns that the requisite mens rea as to participation of this first category of joint criminal enterprise is based on paragraph 105 of the judgement, where the Trial Chamber states that it is satisfied that when the appellant left the hotel he knew that the men were not to be exchanged but were to be killed. Yet this assumption cannot be reached by a reasonable trier of facts and should therefore be dismissed for the following reasons. First, in paragraph 105, the Trial Chamber elucidates on an incident whereby Muslim employees were taken out of the Varda factory. The Trial Chamber situates this incident to have been taken place before the afternoon of June 7, 1992; therefore, before the Drina River incident. However, Your Honours, the events at the Varda factory took place only on the 10th of June, 1992; therefore, after the Drina River incident. And that you may find in paragraph 15 of the amended indictment of the Prosecution. As a consequence, the Trial Chamber misinterpreted this event and could not have accepted that the appellant knew that the particular men were to be killed based on the Varda factory incident. This misinterpretation, Your Honours, also seriously affects the further assessments by the Trial Chamber with respect to the alleged participation of the appellant. In particular, it should also disqualify the Trial Chamber's rejection in paragraph 105, the same paragraph, that it was only when Milan Lukic stopped the cars nearby the Drina River incident that the appellant understood that these men were not to be exchanged. Second, paragraph 105 of the judgement is in contradiction with paragraph 252, already mentioned, where in another context it is mentioned that "there is no basis in the evidence for finding beyond reasonable doubt what specific crimes were committed by the Milan Lukic group which resulted from the assistance ..." The absence of mens rea on the part of the appellant with respect to the element of "a common criminal purpose and joint criminal enterprise" is also clearly envisioned by the testimony of the accused himself, where he in detail tells us what happened at the Drina River incident. I already referred to this citation earlier. Your Honours, in this respect, the Trial Chamber, in paragraph 106, rejects this evidence presented by the accused, referring to the evidence of VG32, namely that the appellant allegedly would have said nothing in response to the pleas by the men. Yet the Trial Chamber is willing to accept, in paragraph 107, the evidence of VG32 and VG14, that nobody was able to stop Milan Lukic. Therefore, even when the appellant was not to be believed on this point - let us take the position of the Trial Chamber in this respect - this leaves untouched the argument that no reasonable Court could have accepted participation in a joint criminal enterprise on the part of the appellant, when considering the evidence given by VG32 and VG14. In conclusion, these citations from the Trial Chamber judgement itself indicate that it erred in facts with respect to the acceptance of mens rea on the part of the appellant and especially with respect to paragraphs 105, as well as paragraphs 107, where it is rejected that the appellant was powerless to stop Milan Lukic from killing the Muslim men. This conclusion is reinforced by the testimonies given by both the two survivors, and that of the accused himself, which were overlooked by the Trial Chamber. Importantly, paragraph 107 of that judgement is a clear acknowledgment by the Trial Chamber of the fact that these witnesses gave evidence of their impression that throughout the entire incident there was nobody around Milan Lukic who could have affected him or his decisions and orders in any meaningful way. That's the citation literally from the Trial Chamber decision. This observation was, therefore, clearly undisputed by the Trial Chamber, yet totally negated. Therefore, no reasonable Trial Chamber could have accepted mens rea on that part of the appellant when reading his statement before the Chamber delivered on 23 October 2001, especially the circumstance described by the appellant himself, that he tried to prevent Milan Lukic at the Drina River from killing of the particular persons, indicates that no mens rea existed with respect to the alleged common purpose. Furthermore, this statement indicates that the stop at the Drina River emerged unexpectedly for the appellant. The observation of the Trial Chamber in paragraph 107, last sentence, namely that it was satisfied that the appellant willingly accompanied Milan Lukic and his group, leaves untouched the earlier observation that the two key witnesses stressed that no one around Lukic could have prevented him from pursuing his actions. The Defence holds that this fact, this observation, amounts to an error of fact as well as to a misinterpretation of the requisite element of mens rea for joint criminal enterprise.
