Let me turn shortly to the elaboration by the Appeals Chamber judgement in the Tadic case, with respect to the formulation of mens rea in the context of the first category. In paragraph 228, the Appeals Chamber contemplates as follows: "By contrast, the mens rea element differs according to the category of common design under consideration. With regard to the first category, what is required is the intent to perpetrate a certain crime, this being the shared intent on part of all co-perpetrators." Your Honours, in view of the Prosecutor's evidentiary foundation, namely the first category of joint criminal enterprise and the acceptance of that category by the Trial Chamber, no reasonable Trial Chamber could have accepted mens rea on the part of the appellant in terms of its shared intent, as emphasised by the Tadic appeals judgement. Moreover, in paragraph 105 of the Trial Chamber judgement in this case, it deduces this mental element of shared intent on the part of the appellant from "the evidence of the accused himself ... that he knew that Milan Lukic had committed serious crimes ... in the area of Visegrad." However, prior knowledge of alleged crimes as such cannot justify the acceptance of a shared intent. Furthermore, I already indicated in paragraph 30 of my submissions that on this particular point the Trial Chamber erred in law with respect to the Varda factory incident, which took place after 7 June 1992. In the Simic judgement, already referred to, the Trial Chamber took the comparison between participation in joint criminal enterprise and the requisite mens rea for aiding and abetting. In paragraph 160 of that judgement, the Trial Chamber holds, in delineating this difference, that "The participant in the basic form of joint criminal enterprise must share with the person who physically carries out the crime the state of mind required for that crime; whereas, the person who merely aids and abets must be aware of the essential elements of the crime committed ... but he need not share are that same state of mind." Now, turning to the case of the appellant, it can nowhere be deduced that he shared exactly the same intent as to Mr. Lukic and his group, in terms of the Simic judgement. This conclusion is reinforced by the Ojdanic decision on joint criminal enterprise, in paragraph 26, where it is stressed that this concept, concept of joint criminal enterprise, pertains to the participation in the commission. Mere membership of such an enterprise is not sufficient for liability, according to the Ojdanic decision. Similarly, no reasonable tribunal could have held the appellant liable for the mere act of accompanying the members of the particular Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. criminal enterprise from the hotel to the river on the 7th June 1992. In the event the Appeals Chamber were to accept aiding and abetting, this should lead to a substantial mitigation of the sentence, to which I will return later. But for now it's sufficient to say, in conclusion, that from the perspective of the first category of joint criminal enterprise no reasonable Court could have accepted the existence of mens rea on the part of the appellant, especially not when considering the paragraphs 75, 76, 95, and 305 of the judgement I elaborated on. I turn now to the next issue of error of law and its impact on the Trial Chamber observations, namely the intent -- special intent provided for with respect to the crime of persecution. Here, in addition to the intent necessary for the commission of an ordinary crime, discriminatory intent is required; namely, the will to discriminate against members of a particular national, ethnic, religious, racial or other group. Your Honours, the ICTY Trial Chamber, in both Kupreskic et al. And Kordic and Cerkez et al. ruled that the acts of the accused must be seen as "aimed at singling out and attacking certain individuals on discriminatory grounds" with the ultimate aim of "removal of those persons from the society in which they live alongside the perpetrator, or eventually from humanity itself." In the Blaskic Trial Chamber decision, this specific intent was worded as follows: "The specific intent to cause injury to a human being because he belongs to a particular community or group." Now, two reasons emerge as to error of law regarding this issue, and these are also the implications of these observations on the Trial Chamber conclusions. First of all, the aforementioned legal criteria --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel, I -- we are -- we have to look at the watch from time to time. I realise this is difficult. I think that we can give you until 12.15, but no longer. So please plan your time accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The first reason, the acceptance by the Trial Chamber that the appellant was not a member of the Milan Lukic group nor that he shared the general homicidal intentions of the group, paragraph 95; second, the acceptance by the Trial Chamber that the seven Muslim men were apparently already singled out on the 7th June, before the appearance of the appellant in the Vilina Vlas Hotel, paragraphs 99 and 100 of the judgement; and third, the acceptance by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 305 that the appellant did not take part in the planning of the execution of the five Muslim men "but only became involved at the time when these men were brought to that hotel a short time before they were killed." Your Honours, the use of the term "a short time" in this paragraph 305 already illustrates the improbability of the existence of special intent, as envisioned by the mentioned case law of the ICTY required for the crime of persecution. In sum, these facts derived from the judgement of this case itself justify the conclusion that no reasonable Court could have accepted special intent on the part of the appellant. In this sense, contrary to the argument of the Prosecutor in paragraph 1.9 of the Prosecution respondent's brief, particular findings of facts are established by the Defence for the conclusion that these could not reasonably have been reached by any reasonable Court. And I just mentioned all the paragraphs from the judgement itself. In the Kupreskic trial judgement, the higher threshold of and for mens rea, regarding persecution, compared to other crimes against humanity, was defined as follows: "The mens rea requirement for persecution is higher than for ordinary crimes against humanity, although lower than for genocide." Nowhere in this evidence we find objective arguments of facts for the conclusion that the appellant did not "initially target the individual but, rather, as required for persecution, membership in a specific racial, religious, or political group." This may be derived from paragraph 235 of the Blaskic trial judgement. So it should be established that not only an accused targets an individual but also, and moreover, membership itself of a specific group. Your Honours, this conclusion is reinforced by the following argument: In the Tadic judgement, paragraphs 694, 781, the Trial Chamber held Mr. Dusko Tadic criminally liable for the crime of persecution based on his role in numerous attacks on and forced removal of civilians. Contrary to the Prosecution respondent's brief under paragraph 714 and this reference to the Kupreskic Trial Chamber judgement, the Defence disputes the notion that in general the crime of persecution may consist of a single act. This conclusion finds support in the decision on Defence motion on form of indictment rendered in the Tadic case in 1995, where Trial Chamber II contemplated that "The very nature of criminal acts in respect of which competence is conferred upon, by Article 5, ensures that what is to be alleged will not be one particular act but instead a course of conduct." Secondly, this refutal finds support in the mentioned Kupreskic trial judgement itself, where it is said in paragraph 636 that, in the case of persecution, the discriminatory intent can take multifarious human forms and manifest itself in a plurality of actions, including murder. Therefore, an isolated act as such cannot be subsumed under persecution. In paragraphs 616 and 627 of the Kupreskic decision of 14 January 2000, the Trial Chamber went even further by saying that "Acts of persecution must be evaluated not in isolation but in context by looking at their cumulative effect." The Trial Chamber explicitly refers to the overall consequences on humanity in order to be qualified as persecution. These elements are absent in this specific case, and therefore the Trial Chamber overlooked these criteria. These arguments already denote for reversal of the judgement, and should your Chamber nonetheless accept the notion that the crime of persecution may be confined to one single act, the Defence holds the opinion that this may be only justified in the event of special circumstances; in other words, in case of a rather isolated event from this perspective of the accused, such as the charged Drina River incident with respect to the appellant, the special intent may only be inferred from unequivocal and clear circumstances which leave no doubt whatsoever about the mental state of the accused. Therefore, the Trial Chamber erred by accepting evidence on this only by way of inferences. The criterion of clear evidence of discriminatory intent, in the case of a single act, was also the position taken by the Trial Chamber in the Kupreskic case. In arriving at the conclusion that special intent existed as to the appellant, the Trial Chamber virtually based this finding, indeed, on one isolated incident, which apparently took place within ten minutes after arrive -- after leaving the hotel on June the 7th. Your Honours, the establishment of mens rea becomes more complex with respect to such a short period of time without any clear and unequivocal inferences. May I draw the attention of your Chamber to paragraph 78 of the judgement, where it is said that the Trial Chamber "is not satisfied that the Prosecution has sufficiently established any of the other incidents relied upon," incidents in which the appellant was alleged to have been involved. I also draw your attention to paragraph 79 of the judgement, where the Trial Chamber, confronted with evidence adduced by the Prosecution, held that it did not accept that evidence. I arrive now at your remark, at your reference to the paragraphs 18 and 19 of the additional Defence brief, with respect to the aspect of command responsibility. The reference to the final report of commissions of experts referred to on that particular point was merely meant as showing that when an evidentiary value in criminal matters is to be attached to the absence of a so-called modus operandi of similar illegal acts, it can be held by way of inference or analogy that its value may be attributed to paragraph 79, in terms of an exculpatory observation. This was also explained in the paragraphs 15 and 16 of the additional Defence reply in appeal. Second, the Trial Chamber erred in law due to the following: In paragraph 254 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber finds that the only reasonable inference available on the evidence is that the victims were singled out for religious or political reasons. On this point, the judgement bears serious inconsistency. Whereas in this paragraph the Trial Chamber connects the appellant with the singling out of the seven men, the paragraphs 99, 100, and 305 assume the non-presence or non-involvement of the appellant with respect to this singling out. Clearly, this may be derived from paragraph 305, where it is accepted by the Court that the appellant did not appear to take part in the planning and execution but only became involved at the time when these men were brought to the hotel. In conclusion, the Defence respectfully prays that the Appeals Chamber reverses the judgement in that the appellant is acquitted for the crime of persecution. For the sake of time, I briefly will touch the mens rea of the crime of murder. The arguments put forward with respect to persecution also count for the refusal of mens rea for the crime of murder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel, may I draw your attention. You have only five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And just make sure that if there are some really important issues to which you would like to draw our attention that, you use the time wisely for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I briefly will illuminate appeal ground number 8, as my last point. Apparently the Prosecution in paragraph 9.8 seems to accept that the invoked argument, special intent as aggravating factor for Count 5, amounting to a violation of non bis in idem, would have been valid in the event of a concurrent conviction for persecution and war crimes. In the mentioned Simic judgement of October 17, the Trial Chamber acknowledged in paragraph 1058, that in addition the persecution charge requires a distinct element, namely discriminatory intent. Accordingly, the Chamber only entered a conviction for persecution and not for deportation concerning the relevant conduct found to constitute the persecutions charge. By way of analogy or reasoning a contrario, it amounts to an error of law when such an materially distinct element as that of special intent is being implemented as an aggravating factor for murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war and/or a crime against humanity. This especially counts as the appellant was found criminally liable as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise to persecute seven men at the Drina River. Your Honours, these submissions arrive at the announced new sentencing circumstance. I draw your attention to Article 24, Section 1 of the Statute and Rule 101(B) under (iii), requiring the Chamber to take into account the general practice regarding prison sentences in the courts of the former Yugoslavia. In this respect, a report was published by Amnesty International on the 1st of October, 2003, indicating that Mr. Lukic was convicted on 29 September of this year to 20 years' imprisonment by a Serbian national court for implication in the killing of 16 men, 16 Muslim men, in October 1992. The Defence is able to submit this report, if Your Honours so wish it. It should therefore be observed that Mr. Vasiljevic was de facto imposed the same prison sentence as Mr. Milan Lukic, in the words of the Trial Chamber in this case, the leader of a paramilitary organisation and instigator of many crimes. This qualification was not only adjusted by the Prosecution in this case but also by the Court verdict against Mr. Lukic in Serbia. This observation, therefore, seems undisputed and a fact of common knowledge in terms of Rule 94 and 107 of the Rules of Procedure. Alternatively, in the event the convictions were to be upheld, the Defence respectfully prays the Appeals Chamber to substantially mitigate the imposed sentence due to the disproportionality between this sentence and that imposed on Mr. Lukic, bearing in mind the latter's responsibility and role in several alleged crimes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Knoops. What I would suggest is that we spend a few minutes now to ask questions of the counsel for the defendant, and I will invite my colleagues in a moment to start that. But I just have a tiny question of terminology, which either of you might clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: The names Varda and Partizan, do they refer to the same company or factory or to different ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I know, those are two different companies, companies that were not privately owned. Varda was a socially or state-owned enterprise in Visegrad. I remember a question asked by Mr. Groome of Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic, whether the Pecikoza enterprise was under Varda or Partizan. But neither is true. Pecikoza was a privately-owned enterprise. These two companies were located in Visegrad and employed a large number of workers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now I will turn to my colleagues and invite them to ask questions. I call on my colleague Judge Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I would have a number of questions emanating from your contribution, but I want to limit myself to one special -- and maybe it can be clarified or maybe it's a misunderstanding from my side. You mentioned in the context of the question whether or not there was a substantial contribution on the part of the appellant, paragraph 302 of the judgement as -- in support of your submission. But isn't it true that it reads there: "This accused was not a commander, his crimes were -- geographically were limited, and there is no evidence that his acts encouraged other offenders (other than as found in relation to the Drina River incident) or affected other victims of such crimes within the broader context of the conflict"? So if you please could elaborate what the impact of this paragraph is on your submission as to the contribution of the accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for this question. The Defence holds that indeed paragraph 302 should be read in a broader context, but apparently the Court accepts the notion that Mr. Vasiljevic did not encourage other offenders, in view of the Court, other than on this particular day, the 7th June 1992. Yet, when reading the paragraphs 72 to 79, the Trial Chamber seems to deduce from the previous context between the appellant and the group of Milan Lukic an argument for his alleged participation in a joint criminal enterprise, an inculpatory argument. And it is the view of the Defence that once you accept in paragraph 302 that he did not encourage other offenders before the Drina River incident, it's not logical that you nonetheless extract from the previous context between the appellant and Mr. Lukic an inculpatory argument. I hope the question is answered by this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could I invite my other colleagues to ask questions should they want -- Judge Guney.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Domazet, during your submissions, you said that the appellant was not an informer at an important moment of Milan Lukic or his group. On the other hand, Mr. Knoops also during his submissions contested the participation -- the continued participation of the appellant to an important extent in the joint criminal enterprise. What exactly do you mean when you refer to "important moments in the course of the events and in this particular case"? Would you be kind enough to elaborate and clarify your submissions in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. When I said that there was no evidence that the appellant was some sort of an informer of this group, I provided all the evidence in support of such a submission but there is one thing that speaks for itself and that is that the -- and that is reflected in the sentence is that the appellant was convicted for the Drina River incident of the 7th of June. I should like in any event to try to prove that everything that happened after that, the most gravest crimes occurred after the 7th of June, committed by Milan Lukic's group or others, and I think that this cannot be put as part of the responsibility of Mr. Vasiljevic, especially as after the 14th of June he wasn't physically in Visegrad any longer. On the other hand, I noticed in one of the questions put by His Honour, the President, regarding a Muslim woman who was denied medical treatment. That is a doctor that couldn't or didn't want to assist her. That fact does exist, but this was an event that occurred after the 14th, after the crime in Pionirska Street, and that really has nothing at all to do with Vasiljevic. And I think we have to observe the period up to the 6th of June when dealing with the Vasiljevic case. I don't know whether I have answered your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I will now call on my colleague, Judge Shahabuddeen, to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Knoops, I'm obliged to you for an interesting argument. I wonder, however, whether I may put to you a question concerning the factual aspects of a matter. At page 50 of the transcript, line 13 you are recorded as having said something to the effect that it was only when Milan Lukic stopped the car near the Drina River that the appellant understood that these men were not to be exchanged. Could -- could you indicate very roughly what is the distance between where the car stopped and the river bank where the men were -- were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you for this question. I myself was not personally at the scene or have ever envisioned the scene. Mr. Domazet, as I understood, he went to see there, so perhaps if you allow, I can ask my learned colleague what exactly the distance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, are you in a position to help?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In my opinion, it's about 100, 150 or -- 150 metres between a road and the bank of river. You have in evidence - I think that is Prosecution evidence 18 - a picture from this, but it's my opinion -- I was there. Maybe 50 metres more or less, but it's a distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And what proportion of that distance did the appellant walk?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: This distance, except just a place where they were shooting, 10 or 15 metres, yes, he was with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That is my impression also. Would you say, then, that he walked towards the river bank after it became clear to him that the men were not to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could you help me on another point. This arises from Mr. Knoops's submission, that -- at page 52, line 3 of the transcript. I think the statement there is that the appellant said that he tried to prevent Milan Lukic at the Drina River from killing -- from the killing of a particular person. Would you say that a reasonable implication of that evidence is that the appellant agreed to the killing of the other persons?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I didn't understand this. I think that Mr. Vasiljevic pleaded for all the victims, but he knew very well one of them, Mr. Meho Dzavic, his colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And this is an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you know, a Trial Chamber in that station said that he didn't tell nothing to Milan Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I thank you. I thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: It's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I thank my distinguished colleague Judge Shahabuddeen, and I would now like to ask a question or two. The first one is this: The first one pertains to the question whether there can be some kind of a reasonable inference available on the evidence that in fact Mitar Vasiljevic by his actions intended that the seven men be killed. The appellant, as we all know, denies having had knowledge that the men were to be killed when he left the hotel, but he admits in paragraph 81 of the Defence appeal brief that he had such knowledge after the car stopped and the seven men were ordered to move Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. towards the Drina River. Could Mr. Knoops perhaps explain to the Court why it would be unreasonable to infer from Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic's actions of walking with a rifle and standing, say, 10, 15 metres from the place of the execution, that he intended the seven Muslim men to be killed. I will then have another question after you have answered this one. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, for this question. First of all - and that also relates to the question of Judge Shahabuddeen - I think that distinction should be made between, on the one hand, the moment when the appellant knew what was going to happen and, on the other hand, his intention. According to the case law, both of the ICTY Trial Chamber but also the ICTR - I refer to the case -- the judgement of 21 May 1999 in the Kayishema and Ruzindana case - the Trial Chamber found that the standard of mens rea required for murder is intentional and premeditated killing. Now, the Defence holds that indeed when the car -- the car stopped, apparently the appellant became aware what was really going to happen there, but that does not conclusively lead to the observation, not even by way of inference, that his mens rea fulfilled the requirement of intentional and premeditated killing. So the Defence holds that the Trial Chamber overlooked the distinction between, on the one hand, the awareness on the part of the appellant from the moment the car stopped - on the one hand - and on the other hand, the requirements for murder. So even, in other words, to put it otherwise -- even when your Chamber were to accept that Mr. Vasiljevic, the appellant, knew that the men were to be killed, that is not sufficient to conclude that he participated in the crime of murder, due to the absence of conclusive evidence for the element of intentional and premeditated killing and that the mere fact that he knew from that moment -- only on that moment what was going to happen may be seen as an inference for the Trial Chamber but without additional inferences or evidence, no reasonable Court could have reached the conclusion that the criteria for murder were fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel. I would like now to ask you a question which draws on your argument today, on the question of aiding and abetting. If I understood your argument - and you invoked the Tadic appeals decision - you spoke of the requirement of a substantial effect on the commission of a crime. And what I would like to ask you is this: If a person who is armed stands 10 or 15 metres from a place of an execution which is carried out by three persons, does this not suggest some substantial assistance to the perpetration of the crime by the very fact that victims would be discouraged or prevented from escaping? Could you elaborate on that a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, for this question. In general, I agree with your observation, but I would like to make two remarks. First of all, the appellant denies that he was in the possession of a gun, and only if the Appeals Chamber were to accept the testimony of the two witnesses to that extent, of course your observation bears merit. However, the Defence holds the opinion that the evidence provided to that extent is not conclusive. But secondly, if your Appeals Chamber were to accept, despite the arguments of the Defence, that the appellant was in the possession of a weapon at the Drina river bank and were to believe the witness to that point, you should also believe the two witnesses saying that nobody was able to prevent Mr. Lukic from doing what he did. Now, the Defence already referred in the appeal briefs that it is very difficult and quite improbable to split the two witness statements like the Trial Chamber did. They believed for some part the statements of the witnesses; of another part they accepted the fact that these witnesses were mistaken. Now, even if your Trial Chamber were to accept that a witness statement is to be split and to be selected into the evidence for a certain part, with this particular argument the Defence holds the opinion that even if your Court were to accept -- were to accept that Mr. Vasiljevic was in the possession of a gun at the Drina River, he did not substantially contribute the events which happened there, due to the statements of the two witnesses. I hope I have addressed the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that Judge Shahabuddeen has another question, and I call upon him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just another question, Mr. President. This is a follow-up from something suggested by the question asked by our distinguished President. Mr. Knoops, my impression is that your thesis is -- that proof of a substantial fact has to be made in the case of a charge for aiding and abetting. What I'm not clear about is whether that is absolutely correct. Is it perhaps the case that proof of a substantial effect has to be made in the case of a charge relating to the full events, the position being this: That in the case of the full offence, the Prosecution must prove intent; the Prosecution in the case of a charge for aiding and abetting has only to prove knowledge but not intent. However, it must fill the vacuum, as it were, by proving in the case of aiding and abetting that there was a substantial effect of the actions of the accused in relation to the accomplishment of the ultimate objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for asking me this question. It is indeed the opinion of the Defence that proof of a substantial fact should be made both with respect to participation in a joint criminal enterprise but also with respect to the charge for aiding and abetting while acknowledging that the latter form may be conducted by way of omission. May I point you to paragraph 160 of the Simic trial judgement, which recently was rendered, in October 2002 [sic], where the Trial Chamber explained the difference between participation in a joint criminal enterprise and participation by way of aiding and abetting and by stressing that the person who merely aids and abets must be aware of the essential elements of the crime committed but need not share the same state of mind. It may be inferred that the contribution, with respect to aiding and abetting, should equally be substantial, in line with -- with being aware of all the essential elements of the crime committed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Knoops. Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen. Thank you, Mr. Knoops. If there are no further questions - and this is my understanding - the Court will now rise, and we will sit again at 2.00 p.m. This afternoon to hear the argument of the Prosecution. So I thank the counsel for their help to the Court this morning. The session is adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.41 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. [Microphone not activated] We will now move on to hear the response by the Prosecution, and I will come --

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Before I get started, I'd like to give a brief outline of how we intend to proceed in our response this afternoon. We've handed up a Prosecution order of appearance and our arguments in response. I understand Your Honours have a copy of that. Good. You'll see from that that I'll be addressing you on the first five grounds of appeal. I'm taking them in a slightly different order in which they were presented in argument this morning, and that's for twofold reasons: Firstly, because we feel that we can present our arguments more efficiently and effectively in response in this order; and secondly, in doing so we hope to address specifically the areas which Your Honour, President Judge Meron, has identified as the ones truly forming the basis for this appeal. I'll be dealing in the following order: Ground 2, Vasiljevic's relationship with the Milan Lukic paramilitary group; ground 3, general requirements for Articles 3 and 5; then I'll be turning to the crux of the case, concerning Drina River incident, ground 1; and in the application of the load of the facts for murder and inhumane acts, that is, grounds 4 and 5. At that juncture, Your Honours, I'll will turning to my colleague, Ms. Michelle Jarvis, who will be addressing you on the arguments in response on ground 6, persecution, and ground 7, individual criminal responsibility. And she'll be dealing mainly with the errors of law which were highlighted this morning by the appellants. And finally, my colleague, Mr. Steffen Wirth, will address you on ground 8, sentence. Turning first to the appellant's second ground of appeal, and this is essentially that the Trial Chamber erred in its assessment of Vasiljevic's relationship with the Milan Lukic group, the paramilitary group led by Milan Lukic. In our submission he's not shown that these findings were unreasonable, and we ask you to dismiss this ground because no appealable error of facts or fact have been established. In fact, in our submission, far from being unreasonable, the Trial Chamber's findings on the relationship were more than reasonable. Indeed, you could describe them as circumspect. How did the Trial Chamber characterise that relationship? Not that he was a member of the Milan Lukic group, nor, except as otherwise found in the judgement, that he participated in the group's crimes in Visegrad, but rather - and I'm quoting now from the judgement at paragraphs 75 and 95 - that he had "some association with the group." He was "a ready source of local information for the group about the location of Muslims in the area of Visegrad and he gave that information to the group with the full realisation that it would be used to persecute Muslims." And finally, that he willingly acted as an informant to that group. Now, in his second ground - and as we heard this morning from Mr. Domazet, he challenges these findings. But before I deal with his challenges to the reasonableness or, as he -- as he puts it, he says "the unreasonableness of these findings", I need to stress at the outset that the Trial Chamber was very careful about how it used these findings regarding his relationship with the Milan Lukic group when it came to examine his criminal responsibility for the Drina River incident. And the reason I say this is because at times when I heard the submissions this morning, it seemed that the appellant had not fully appreciated the Trial Chamber's very careful probative or forensic use of these findings. And in particular, in highlighting this alleged inconsistency in the Trial Chamber's findings of -- in paragraph 72 to 79, vis-a-vis paragraphs 302, it seems to us that he's not fully comprehended or recognised how the Trial Chamber used these findings in the Drina River incident. Critically, the Trial Chamber drew no inference that that association on its own was sufficient to find that he shared the general homicidal intentions of the group, nor on its own was it sufficient to establish his discriminatory, his persecutory mental state during the Drina River; and nor, and despite the contrary submission to the appellant, did it appear to have an impact on the sentencing of the Trial Chamber. Rather, the Trial Chamber inferred his intention to kill on the day of the Drina River incident, based on the circumstances of that incident. And I'll delve more into this when we come to ground 4. Likewise, the Trial Chamber treated his association with the group, including that he gave information to the group about the location of local Muslims, as not on its own sufficient to establish that he had discriminatory state of mind during the Drina River incident. Albeit, it was one factor in the whole factual matrix from which the Trial Chamber found he had discriminatory intent that day. And my colleague, Ms. Jarvis, will deal more specifically with this point when we turn to ground 6 on persecution. The Trial Chamber's main probative use of the findings about this relationship was to establish his connection to the armed conflict and the wider attack against the civilian population. And when I come to address you more specifically on ground 3, I'll show that the use in this regard cannot have been said to have been unreasonable. Now, I'd like to turn to the findings themselves and the arguments especially that he raised this morning. He argues essentially that the assessment by the Trial Chamber of the relationship was wrong, and he does this by attacking in a sort of piecemeal fashion each of the bodies of evidence, each of the strands of evidence upon which the Trial Chamber relied. Essentially he says, "Well, this strand, this piece of evidence can't prove the relationship with the group or that piece of evidence can't show it either." And in our submission, this is an artificial approach because it fails to recognise that the Trial Chamber's findings on the relationship were based on a combination of several bodies of evidence that led it to make search different but related findings about the relationship. It was really a package of evidence and findings. I should also stress one thing in light of his submissions this morning that the Trial Chamber did not base its findings about his association with the Milan Lukic group and especially his being a ready and willing source of information for it about local Muslims, knowing it would be used to persecute them. It didn't base it solely on his prior acquaintance, him having known Milan Lukic and the other men before. That's not the basis for the finding. Rather, it was four things, four main bodies of evidence that the Trial Chamber relied on in order to infer and conclude about the relationship. Firstly, his detailed trial testimony. He gave very detailed testimony regarding his knowledge of the group, the members, the structure, the activities, and the like; the second aspect, his prior kum relationship with Milan Lukic, aspects of what we could call his post-1992 relationship with Milan Lukic, and his acquaintance with the other men in the group; the third body of evidence comes from his participation with Milan Lukic and the other men in the search of the Muslim house in Musici one week prior to the Drina incident; and the fourth piece of evidence upon which the Trial Chamber made a clear factual finding, the comment overheard by VG14, when the car stopped at Sase near the Drina River and at that point Vasiljevic pointed to a house and told Lukic it was a Muslim house. And in our submission, it was not unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to rely on and draw inferences from the combination of these four strands of evidence in order to find his association with the group and to reach the factual findings that it did about his relationship with that group. In our response brief, we've made extensive arguments in response to his various challenges to each of these facts, so this afternoon I can be quite short form in my response to the various challenges that he makes to each of these findings, but I would like to make some brief points on each one. On the first matter, about his detailed testimony of the group and the activities, he tries now to put a very positive complexion on Vasiljevic's detailed trial testimony, and he basically says, "Well, this shouldn't be seen -- this should be seen as a sign of cooperation with the Court, not interpreted against him or held against him." In our submission, there was nothing unreasonable in the Trial Chamber regarding his detailed level of knowledge, especially the detail he gave about all the members and the structure of the group, as indicating that he had a closer form of relationship with the group than merely being someone who picked up this information as a local citizen of Visegrad, either during or even after the relevant time. This morning, Mr. Domazet said that the reason why other witnesses didn't testify about these details is because they were scared to and they had other reasons not to provide as much information to the Court; whereas, Vasiljevic was really trying to provide as much as he could. In our submission, this -- his submission about the witnesses is entirely speculative. Well may Vasiljevic have told the Court a lot, but it what he was able to tell the Court which speaks volumes. And in this respect, the Court was not -- the Trial Chamber was not unreasonable to rely on it in the way that it did. Nor, in our submission, was it unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to have treated his prior kum relationship with Milan Lukic and his acquaintance with the other men in the group as a further strand of evidence, a further body of evidence from which to make findings about his relationship with the Milan Lukic group. A lot of evidence was heard from both sides during the trial about the strength of this kum relationship in Serbian culture, and indeed Vasiljevic agreed he had a close relationship with Milan Lukic in his interview of 16 November 2000, at page 33, and in the admissions of the parties at paragraph 3(Y). As he did in the trial, he now on appeal has tried to diminish the strength of that relationship. He's saying, "Well, it was with the Lukic family and he was not personally close with Lukic and there was this age difference and Lukic had got --had left Visegrad after school. These matters were all before the Trial Chamber and considered, and it certainly doesn't show that the Trial Chamber was unreasonable in its findings in this respect. Nor, in our submission, was it unreasonable for the Trial Chamber and despite Vasiljevic's assertions to the contrary, to the effect that he tried to avoid Milan Lukic after the Drina River, to consider the fact that he was best man to Lukic and then godfather to his daughter some three or four or five years after Drina River incident, was indicative of some closer relationship between he and Milan Lukic at the relevant time. And Mr. Domazet said this morning that he -- that this fact considerably damaged his case. In actuality, this was really one piece -- one strand of evidence from which the Trial Chamber drew this final conclusions about his relationship. But also in relation to this particular finding, the Trial Chamber was very careful about how it used this particular evidence of his, what we could call, post-1992 association with Milan Lukic. The Trial Chamber at paragraph 75 said that it "raised a suspicion of a closer relationship with Milan Lukic and the group and then only because he allowed it to continue despite his knowledge of Milan Lukic's very serious criminal activity." So in other words, the fact that he didn't break the relationship says something about the strength of the relationship before. And this is not unreasonable. Finally -- excuse me, thirdly, the third strand of evidence that the appellant attacked this morning and which, in our submission, were quite reasonable for the Trial Chamber to have drawn, concern the Trial Chamber's findings about the search in Musici. The appellant has not shown that it was unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to find that during the search in -- of the Muslim house in Musici in late May that Vasiljevic stood guard outside the house armed with an automatic rifle while Lukic and seven to ten armed men searched it. The differences that he pointed out in his appellant's brief between the two witnesses' evidence do not establish that the Trial Chamber erred in regarding them as reliable and credible, and we note even that Vasiljevic himself at trial, at transcript 2060, agreed that they were quite correct in their testimony and he was glad that they hadn't embellished or exaggerated his role in it. The discrepancies that he alluded to are hardly surprising after the lapse of 9 years from the incident to when the witnesses gave evidence. And the fourth and most important point, what is most important, shows that the Trial Chamber did not err is that both witnesses agreed on the central point, and that is that he stood guard outside the house with his rifle to prevent the occupants from leaving. He says this is just the impression of the witnesses, and the Prosecution asks: How can any other interpretation be gained when this was the evidence? This morning he also said -- in his submissions, Mr. Domazet said that the most telling feature about why he couldn't have been an informant for the group was because he knew that VG59 and his brother were reserve policemen and he didn't tell Lukic this at the time. Your Honours, there may be many reasons why he would not tell on this particular occasion, on this particular family -- he'd been to school with -- he and his wife had been to school with VG59 and 55 and he himself said he was quite embarrassed to be there. Well, there could be many reasons why he would not inform on this family. It does not show that he was not otherwise an informant or acted as an informant to the group on other occasions, with other people. Finally, the final body of evidence which the Trial Chamber relied upon to make its ultimate findings about the relationship with the Milan Lukic group was this conversation between Vasiljevic and Milan Lukic Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which VG14 overheard in the car when it stopped at Sase near the Drina River. In our submission, the Trial Chamber was not unreasonable to find that he was a ready source of information to assist the group to locate Muslims in Visegrad - they called it an informant status - based on his comment to Milan Lukic that when they arrived at the Drina River, that "that house was a Muslim house," especially given the timing of this comment, when it was made, and the context in which it was made, especially his close relationship with Milan Lukic. In conclusion on this ground, Your Honours, in our submission the appellant has not shown that the Trial Chamber made errors of fact as to his relationship with the Milan Lukic group, and we ask that this ground be dismissed. I'll turn now to his third ground, in which he challenges the findings on threshold elements of Articles 3 and 5. This morning he was rather brief in dealing with his arguments on this particular ground, and he more or less interwove many of his arguments on ground 3 into ground 2, so what I propose to do is address very shortly on this ground and in particular to focus on some of the issues -- the issues that the President pointed out in opening this morning concerning the various areas that he raised in his brief. Essentially, as we see it, on this ground he has three lines of argument. Firstly, he challenges some of the Trial Chamber's factual findings, and in this respect mostly in paragraphs 46 and 48, as to his relationship with the Milan Lukic -- with Milan Lukic and the men in his group, and especially his knowledge at the time of the Drina River incident of their criminal activities, as well as his role in the search at Musici. Because most of these arguments actually overlap and repeat on ground 2, I can be brief. I've already gone into some detail when dealing with ground 2 on most of these arguments. The second line of argument that he makes in ground 3 is that in his appellant's brief he appears to have taken issue with certain of the Trial Chamber's findings as to the existence of the widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population of Visegrad. Finally, in his brief he challenges the Trial Chamber's conclusions under Articles 3 and 5, that he had the necessary nexus or connection to the armed conflict and the wider attack against the civilian population for Articles 3 and 5 convictions. So I'll deal with them quite briefly in that order. I've already argued that it was not unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to have found that Vasiljevic knew Milan Lukic well. In our submission, he also cannot succeed in showing the unreasonableness of the Trial Chamber's finding that he knew the other men associated with Milan Lukic. And I invite Your Honours to look at the transcript at pages 1985 to 1998. And it's clear from his testimony at trial that he knew all the men in the group before 1992 except VGD4, whom he began to know when the group came to town in 1992. He names various ones who were all originally from Visegrad, VG3, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 9. He mentions that he was the kum of VGD10, and that he was distantly related to VGD5 and 6, and so on and so forth. And in light of this very solid evidence, in our submission there's no error. He also argues - and he spent some time this morning developing this argument - that the Trial Chamber erred in paragraph 46 when it found that Vasiljevic knew that Milan Lukic and his group had committed serious crimes. I'll return to this point later, because it comes to the fore again when I come to the Drina River ground, ground 1, and it's related to the finding that Vasiljevic knew on the 7th of June 1992 when he left the hotel that the seven men were to be taken out and killed. But for his third ground, the issue is relevant to whether his acts had the requisite nexus with the armed conflict for the purposes of Article 3 and that he knew his acts formed part of the wider attack for the purposes of Article 5. Now, this morning he said -- or emphasised that the appellant didn't know at the time of the Drina River incident that Milan Lukic had committed crimes, that he learnt this only later. We agree that the relevant time to assess his knowledge about this issue, that is, to establish his awareness of the wider context of his actions, is indeed the 7th of June, 1992, but in our submission the Trial Chamber was not unreasonable to find when he took part in the Drina River incident he knew by then that Milan Lukic and his men had committed serious crimes. And I invite you to look at the transcript, references 1979 to 1998. In brief, firstly, he was present and he'd seen what Milan Lukic and some of his men had done in Musici a week before the incident. But secondly, he was told by Stanko Pecikoza about Milan Lukic's serious criminal activity in the car trip to the hotel just half an hour before he joined Lukic and the two other men in taking the seven Muslim men at gunpoint to the banks of the Drina River. In addition to the reference -- the transcript reference, I think it's transcript 2105, I also invite Your Honours to look at Exhibit 15.1, page 87, which is his interview on this -- on this issue. On this evidence, the Trial Chamber made no error in finding that Vasiljevic knew by the 7th of June that Milan Lukic and his group had committed serious crimes. As for his arguments -- challenges to the Trial Chamber's findings about mistreatment of non-Serbs in Visegrad, I won't dwell long on this, because he -- he hasn't developed it much in his argument this morning, and we in fact noticed that it's not part -- it was not a part of his Notice of Appeal. And indeed, he never sought leave to -- to add these as grounds of appeal. We would suggest that this would be enough to reject these arguments in limine. But even if you were to entertain these arguments that he's made against the Trial Chamber's finding of the widespread and systematic attack against the non-Serb civilian population of Visegrad, in our submission his arguments have not established that the Trial Chamber was unreasonable to find, based on extensive evidence before it of the attack against the -- excuse me, the attack against and the mistreatment of the non-Serb Muslim population of Visegrad. And we ask you to dismiss these arguments. The final line of challenge raised by the appellant on this ground concerning Articles 3 and 5 concern the Trial Chamber's findings that his act had sufficient nexus to the armed conflict and the wider attack. And again, he hasn't gone into great detail on this this morning. So briefly, just to state our position in response, the appellant has not established it was unreasonable of the Trial Chamber to have found for Article 3 that his acts were closely related to the armed conflict. Indeed, in this respect, it was not unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to have relied on its earlier findings as to his relationship with the Milan Lukic group, as establishing his close association with the Serb paramilitaries and thus providing the relevant nexus to the armed conflict and accordingly finding that its acts were committed in furtherance of and under the guise of the armed conflict. Likewise, the appellant has not established that it was unreasonable for the Trial Chamber to find for the purposes of Article 5 that his acts comprised part of the widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population of Visegrad and that he knew of the attack and that his actions formed part of it. At trial he agreed knowing generally about crimes against and the mistreatment of Muslims in Visegrad. He agreed he was present the week before Musici and Stanko had told him about Lukic's involvement in some very serious crimes during the drive to the Vilina Vlas Hotel. In summary on this ground, Your Honours, in our submission, the Trial Chamber's findings under Articles 3 and 5, that his acts were sufficiently closely related to the armed conflict and formed part of the wider context of the attack against the civilian population and that he had knowledge that his acts formed part thereof cannot have been said to have been unreasonable, and we ask you to dismiss this ground. I'd like to turn now to the crux of the case, the Drina River incident. In his first ground of appeal, he's challenged the Trial Chamber's factual findings about the Drina River incident. And I'll be addressing those in just a moment. In grounds 4 and 5, he challenges the Trial Chamber's application of the law on murder and inhumane acts to the facts found by the Trial Chamber, and I'll get to that after I've finished on ground 1. And then as I said in my opening, Ms. Jarvis will address the application of the law on persecution to the Trial Chamber's factual findings about the Drina River incident. At the outset, his arguments are really conclusions which he says the Trial Chamber should have drawn from the evidence, not that no reasonable Trial Chamber on the evidence before it could have reached those factual findings as to his criminal participation in the Drina River incident. And in our submission, since he's not met the standard of review for errors of fact, we ask you to dismiss ground 1. He's raised four main arguments on ground 1, and I'll address them in the order that he addressed them this morning: Firstly, the Trial Chamber's finding that he was armed; secondly, the Trial Chamber's findings on some other points concerning the Drina River incident and some discrepancies he points out between Witnesses 14 and 32; thirdly, the Trial Chamber's findings as to Vasiljevic's mens rea; and fourthly, the Trial Chamber's treatment of the evidence of VG79, which shows that he stopped some 10 to 15 metres from the river. Turning first to the finding that Vasiljevic was armed. In our submission, the Trial Chamber was not unreasonable to find, on the basis of VG14 and VG32, that Vasiljevic was armed with an automatic rifle at both the hotel and at the Drina River. This morning he's highlighted the inconsistencies between the evidence of VG14 and 32, especially that VG14 saw Vasiljevic with an automatic rifle in the hotel lobby while VG32 only saw Vasiljevic had a gun when he left the hotel, was getting in the car, and he looked back up at the entrance of the hotel and he saw Vasiljevic coming down with the gun. He also points out that in an earlier statement VG14 had called the gun a semi-automatic. Now, Mr. Domazet said this morning that it was -- it's impossible for one witness not to notice the gun and the other one to have noticed the gun, and he says that the inconsistencies between the witnesses on the gun, whether Vasiljevic had a gun in the lobby or not, as well as their evidence of hearing three clicks down by the riverside at the Drina River, demonstrate that they were, I think he said, motivated to give false evidence, that somehow they were deliberately trying to strengthen the evidence against Vasiljevic, and they fabricated seeing Vasiljevic with a gun at the hotel and the river. These submissions are totally speculative. The finding that he was armed when he left the hotel and at the river were not unreasonable. It's of no consequence that VG32 did not notice Vasiljevic had a gun in the lobby, especially since VG14 described the gun in evidence as having the gun "right next to him," and he motioned to his side. And I invite Your Honours to look at the transcript, page 457, and to even view the court video of the witness's evidence in this regard on the 13th of September, 2000. The critical point is that both witnesses saw him with an automatic rifle by the time he left the hotel. I also would like to turn briefly to his argument that it's unlikely -- to the effect that it's unlikely that he had a gun on this occasion, when witnesses didn't see him with a gun at other times in June, and he sort of piggybacks an argument onto that and he highlighted it this morning, that it's beyond doubt that he didn't get his gun back following his arrest during that short time in 29 May to 1 June, and he says especially since he's no longer in the TO. In our submission, even -- even if he gave up his gun when he was arrested during this period in late May for three days, it is quite possible that he got it back on his release. We only have his word on that. It's also not correct to say that he wouldn't have got his gun back because he was no longer in the TO, for that reason. Because if we see the transcript -- the cross-examination of Mr. Groome on this point was basically that his cleaning job, which he'd got after he was released from that three days in jail, was basically like a -- a commuted -- a commuted sentence. So it was really TO duties in another form. Besides, he could have got access to a gun from a number of places or even at the Vilina Vlas Hotel that day. The point is that he could have got a gun from a number of places. In this respect, his argument does not show that the Trial Chamber was unreasonable to find that he was armed at the hotel and during the Drina River incident based on the evidence of the two eyewitnesses. In terms of the other discrepancies that he's highlighted this morning, between VG14 and 32 - I plan only to address one of them, because we've dealt with most of them in our brief, and that's the one where VG32 did not recall Vasiljevic saying anything as the men were marched from the car and pleading for their lives, nor when the men were at the river bank, when they were lined up at the bank; whereas, on the other hand, VG14 heard in the moments -- in the seconds before the shots Meho Dzavic plead with Vasiljevic not to shoot his old colleague and Vasiljevic replied that he didn't know him. In our submission, this alleged inconsistency, as they call it, doesn't show the Trial Chamber was unable to rely on these two witnesses as to Vasiljevic's role in the whole incident. It's little wonder that in the moment that they believed that they would be executed that their memories don't exactly accord, and it certainly doesn't show, as he said, that VG14 was lying. I want to turn now to a very important issue in this case, and that is the Trial Chamber's findings on Vasiljevic's mens rea and to deal specifically with the arguments that he's made this morning and his brief on that. In our submission, the Trial Chamber was not unreasonable to find at paragraph 105, from all the circumstances, from all the facts that when they left the hotel that Vasiljevic knew the men would be killed and not exchanged. The evidence for that: Based on his relationship with Milan Lukic and the other men in the group, he knew by then that they'd engaged in some serious criminal activity. He himself had taken part with Lukic and his men in the search at Musici a week before. And in the car journey to the Vilina Vlas Hotel that day, just half an hour before, Stanko Pecikoza had told him that Lukic had taken people out of Stanko's factory and mistreated them and from the Varda factory and killed them. Indeed, that was why Stanko was looking for Lukic, according to Vasiljevic, because he wanted to have a word with him about the serious criminal activity that Lukic was engaging in. And I invite Your Honours to look at transcript page 2103 to 2105 and the interview, Prosecution Exhibit 15.1, page 87, for this conversation that Stanko had had -- the information that Stanko had told Vasiljevic. Now, there is another fact by the Trial Chamber, a fact found by the Trial Chamber, which confirms Vasiljevic's knowledge at the time he left the hotel as to the fate of these men, and it's this: It was not disputed that Lukic, as he drove the car from the Vilina Vlas Hotel, he turned right at the crossroads as Sase and after travelling 500 to 600 metres down the road, he stopped the car. The Trial Chamber accepted and found as a fact, based on VG14's evidence, that when the car stopped at that point, the conversation between Vasiljevic and Lukic was this. He pointed to a Muslim -- to a house and said, "That's a Muslim house." This morning, as Mr. Domazet confirmed, and as can be seen from the trial transcript, the appellant didn't utter a single word at the Vilina Vlas Hotel or, as he says, according to him, during the whole incident. So nothing was said except, "That's a Muslim house." In our -- in our submission, this comment, which the Trial Chamber accepted Vasiljevic made, confirms the Trial Chamber's finding that back at the hotel Vasiljevic knew what was going to happen to these men. Although his testimony was that he -- he said that he -- when he left the hotel, he thought he was going to go and assist in an exchange or to provide moral support to his friend Meho and/or to get a lift home. His story was somewhat equivocal on that point. But essentially it was to assist in the exchange. In light of that, Vasiljevic's comment, when the car stopped at the Drina River is of someone who had no need to question what was going on, why they were not going to the exchange. Why? Because he already knew right back from the hotel that this was the plan, this was to be the fate of the men. Just to clarify a point made this morning by, I think, both Mr. Knoops and Mr. Domazet, or at least Mr. Knoops, the argument was that if he'd -- he was mistaken about the contents of the conversation that Stanko and he had in the car that day because the -- he says the Varda factory incident hadn't yet occurred. And we'd just like to clarify that while the incident on the 10th of June in which Lukic took men from the Varda factory and killed them hadn't occurred, according to Stanko, as related to Vasiljevic and as he told the Court, and as the Trial Chamber found at paragraph 105, Lukic took men out of the Varda factory on several occasions to mistreat or to kill them. In our submission, therefore, the Trial Chamber was not unreasonable in its findings as to his knowledge when Vasiljevic left the hotel, but even if the Trial Chamber erred in this finding that when he left the hotel he knew they'd be killed, what is crystal clear is that when the car stopped and the men were ordered to walk to the Drina River Vasiljevic knew then that they would be killed. This is in no doubt. He says it himself. And then let's see what he did. And this relates to the question asked this morning by His Honour Judge Shahabuddeen. It is not, as Mr. Knoops referred to, mere presence or merely accompanying the group. This is what he did. He walked the seven Muslim men at gunpoint with Lukic and the two others; he walked some 100 metres over the meadow through what were potato fields. It was no easy path. There was no set path through this field. Some three or four minutes of walking, until they got to the bushy area of the -- of the willow-trees, all the while with their guns pointed at the seven men and their safety catches off, guarding them to prevent their escape. He and the other men then pushed through this foliage, this curtain of willow-trees, until they got to that lonely spot which was obscured from the road, which was to be the execution site. The seven men were lined up on the river bank and he stood with the other three behind the seven men lined up, and then after a brief conversation the shots began and five were killed and two managed to survive. In our submission, there can be only one reasonable inference open on the evidence, and that he intended to kill the men. Addressing the argument about -- from which we heard both from Mr. Domazet and Mr. Knoops this morning, about the fact that he couldn't have stopped Lukic and he couldn't -- no one could influence him, I should point out that the Trial Chamber did not accept his evidence in this respect. And the issue for the Trial Chamber, if you look at paragraph 107, is whether he could or he could not stop Lukic is really beside the point because it doesn't explain his very active steps in this criminal enterprise, this significant contribution that he's making to the enterprise to move them down to the river so that they could be killed. I'll just turn to the final argument on ground 1 on the Drina River incident, and that is the Trial Chamber's treatment of VG79's evidence. And in his submission, in the appellant's submission, he says this showed that he stopped 10 to 15 metres from the river. His argument is that the Trial Chamber was wrong to treat VG79's evidence as, as I said, not inconsistent with VG14 and 32 but, rather, that it should have been seen as supporting his defence that once the group got to the immediate place of execution, that is, the strip of land between the willow-trees and the bank of the river, that he turned away and stood about 10 to 15 metres away in amongst the trees. And it's important to deal with this evidence. And in our submission, the Trial Chamber made no error in how it did treat VG79's evidence. To do so, it has to be borne in mind that VG79 was across the river from the whole event on a hill, some 400, 500 metres away, and he was watching this incident through binoculars, which he was sharing with his friend. And he saw seven civilian men, including two friends he recognised among that group, marched from the cars by three and at times four men in uniform. And from where he was, his vantage point he saw seven men lined up on the bank and three people behind them who shot them. And as Mr. Domazet pointed out, when asked in cross-examination why he didn't draw in the fourth person in his sketch, D1, he said, "The fourth individual, he was near a tree, and we couldn't see properly from that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. angle, because on the left-hand side he was probably partly covered by the tree as you go towards the Drina River." Now, if I understand the appellant's argument correctly, he says that VG79 and the sketch, D1, shows conclusively that the fourth man, who he assumes to be Vasiljevic, stopped 10 to 15 metres away from the river in between the trees. However, in our submission, his arguments, especially the distances he gives in his reply brief, do not match the evidence. Firstly, VG79 did not either in his testimony or in his sketch give distances. If you look at the sketch, one glance at it will tell you the sketch is not drawn to scale, because the meadow is made into a very small part; whereas, in fact, it is about 100 metres. What he did say was that seven civilian men were lined up on the bank and the shooters were behind them. But from his angle and distance he couldn't estimate how far the shooters were from the civilian men. Secondly, and critically, he said that from his position, that is, on a hill across the river - so he's looking down and at an angle - his vision of the fourth man was obstructed by trees. It's important to look at VG79 and see out it relates to VG14 and 32 in this respect. In our submission, the Trial Chamber was not unreasonable to see VG79's evidence as being in tandem with VG14 and 32. You'll recall that VG32 estimated the distance between the strip of land -- excuse me, estimated the distance of the strip of land between the willow trees and the bank as, he said, 7 to 8 to 10 metres, and you'll recall a very poignant time when he was walking what he thought were those last metres of his life. VG14 estimated that the shooters were about 5 to 6 metres away from the men standing at the bank. So even if Vasiljevic was partially obscured from VG79's view by this -- by a tree, or part of if tree, foliage, Vasiljevic could not have been more than a couple of metres away from the other shooters. And in view of this, the Trial Chamber was not unreasonable to find that Vasiljevic was standing with the other shooters. It certainly does not reveal he tried at any stage to disengage from the process and it cannot in any way take away from his active participation in the whole event. In conclusion on ground 1, the Drina River incident, in our submission no errors of fact have been established and this ground should be dismissed. I'll turn finally to grounds 4 and 5, and I can deal with those two together, mainly because that's how the appellant has dealt with it in his arguments, the arguments on inhumane acts ride on the arguments of the -- of the murder. And I'll also at the outset say that I'm dealing mainly with the factual findings -- the Trial Chamber's factual findings, and generally speaking the Trial Chamber's application of the law on JCE and murder and inhumane acts to the facts. And my colleague, Ms. Jarvis, will address you more specifically on the legal errors identified by the appellant, especially Mr. Knoops this morning. On grounds 4 and 5: In our submission, the appellant has not established that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that the only inference available on the evidence was that he intended the seven men be killed and that he participated with the others in a joint criminal enterprise to kill them, sharing the intent that they would be killed. Now, in ground 4, he raises two main arguments: Firstly, he challenges the Trial Chamber's findings as to the existence of what they called an understanding amounting to an agreement among Lukic -- among Vasiljevic, Lukic, and the two others to kill the seven Muslim men. And his second major argument is that the Trial Chamber was incorrect to find that the only reasonable inference available on the evidence was that he by his actions intended the seven men to be killed. Coming firstly to the agreement, the understanding amounting to an agreement. If I understand his arguments correctly, they appear to be premised or to assume that the agreement for the purposes of a joint criminal enterprise can't arise extemporaneously or it has to be some sort of express verbal or at least overt one. Ms. Jarvis will deal specifically with the legal arguments, but in short the Tribunal law requires neither a preformulated agreement nor express words in order to find an agreement for a joint criminal enterprise. Now, I briefly want to touch on his argument that he put forward this morning that while the men were detained in the hotel lobby, Lukic was looking for keys, and he says that this proves that Lukic had planned to lock these men into a room and there was no time later to form an agreement. And I want to say two main points about this: Firstly, the evidence about the keys or Lukic's search for keys is equivocal. It does not show that Lukic intended to detain them at the hotel. Indeed, VG32 did recall Lukic asking and looking for some keys and then storming out and saying, "Right, we're going back." But VG14 said that Lukic did find some keys and tried without success to get into the manager's office, so this cannot prove exactly what Lukic had in mind. But more to the point, the most important point is even if Lukic's original plan had been to put them in a room, what's clear is that the plan changed. And in our submission, the Trial Chamber did not err in finding from all the surrounding circumstances that by the time they left the hotel, Lukic, Vasiljevic, and the two others understood and agreed on what to do with these men. And in any event, as I explained when I dealt with ground 1, there can be no doubt that at least by the time the men were ordered from the car and marched to the river by the four of them that the agreement had fully solidified. He has argued that if there had been an agreement before they got in the car or in the car, between Lukic and Vasiljevic, then one or the other witnesses would have -- would have heard it. Again, we need only stress that the agreement does not need to be express, and in fact -- the fact that there was no conversation in the car or when they stopped about what would happen to the men in fact suggests that everyone already knew what was going to happen. The second and last main argument that he makes in ground 4 is that the Trial Chamber was unreasonable to infer his intention to kill and being part of the joint criminal enterprise to kill. And in our submission, he's not established that the Trial Chamber erred in relying on Vasiljevic's acts of participation as signalling his intention to be part of the joint criminal enterprise to kill. And again, I would emphasise - and it relates to a question asked by His Honour Judge Meron earlier this morning to the Defence - I would emphasise that there are three major acts of participation here that he's -- that he's engaged in, and it's not what the appellant said as mere presence. Firstly, preventing the seven Muslim men from fleeing while they were detained at the Vilina Vlas Hotel; secondly, escorting them to the bank of the river and pointing a gun at them in order to prevent escape; and thirdly, standing behind the seven Muslim men who were lined up at the bank with his gun together with the other three offenders shortly before the shooting started. Now, in terms of the -- what happened at the Vilina Vlas Hotel, as we conceded in our response brief, it's true that neither witness actually said he pointed -- Vasiljevic pointed a gun at them. So in this respect, we conceded that the finding in paragraph 209 of the trial judgement that he pointed a gun is inaccurate. You'll recall that Witness 32 recalled that another man was -- was actually pointing the gun at them while they were in the lobby. And Witness 14, he simply said that Vasiljevic had a gun. But in our submission, this error was -- is inconsequential and it certainly doesn't cause any miscarriage of justice. Why? Because the substance of the Trial Chamber's finding was that his presence in the hotel with a gun contributed to prevent the seven men from fleeing the hotel, and there can be no error by the Trial Chamber in this respect. In terms of the second act of participation, if we call it that, escorting them to the bank of the river and pointing the gun at them to prevent escape, the Trial Chamber was not unreasonable to see this as a very significant act of assistance to the criminal enterprise. Despite some minor differences between VG14 and 32 about the formation of the group, was it in a column or was it sort of more bunched up as they moved towards the river, they are both clear about his role that day. Vasiljevic, together with Lukic and the two others, walked the seven men at gunpoint with safeties off, thereby preventing the seven men from escaping. And dealing with his argument this morning that Well, Lukic and the two others were already doing this, so he wasn't really needed. Well, in our submission, this can't be sustained and we have to remember this was a group of seven men that was being basically moved down to the river to their point of execution by four men. Finally, the standing behind the seven Muslim men who were lined up with his gun, together with the other three offenders just before the shooting. In our submission, the Trial Chamber was not unreasonable to view that this standing with the others with his gun, just before the shooting began, to see it as a significant act of assistance to the joint criminal enterprise to kill them. So in summary, with these acts, in our submission it was not unreasonable to find that he participated in the joint criminal enterprise by assisting the three others to commit the agreed crime and by undertaking acts that facilitated the commission of the offence by those three. Dealing with his argument -- I want to get back to his argument that the three men hadn't earlier that day needed his help in arresting the seven men or in getting them to the hotel or indeed, he says, getting them down to the river. Firstly, as I said before, it's difficult to accept this factually, given that there is -- we're talking about four men moving seven men to the -- to the point of their execution. But in any event, in our submission, it's not a question of needing Vasiljevic's assistance in terms of him being an integral, you know, absolutely necessary vital key component of the enterprise but, rather, that he willingly did perform such significant acts of assistance. In other words, he bought into the plan and he was subscribing to the plan. And I don't need to remind Your Honours that obviously for a joint criminal enterprise, the participant doesn't have to play an integral role. So long as it's a -- well, it's a contribution to the JCE. And here we have not just contribution but we have a significant contribution at that. As the appellant, he must show that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have concluded on these facts that he shared the intention of the joint criminal enterprise to kill the men, that is, that another reasonable inference was available. And he has not. In our submission, the only reasonable inference available was that by his actions he intended the seven Muslim men be killed. This morning Mr. Knoops for the appellant pointed out that -- that this is in some way inconsistent, he says, with the finding in paragraph 75, whereby the Trial Chamber found that his association with the Milan Lukic group was not sufficient by itself to find that he shared the general homicidal intentions of the group. And that's exactly right. But on the evidence in relation to this crime, for this day and what he did then, the Trial Chamber did find that he shared the intention of the group to kill. And on the evidence before it, it was not unreasonable for it to have done so. Likewise, the Trial Chamber was not unreasonable to classify him as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise, not merely an aider and abettor. And I don't -- I won't go into this in great detail because Ms. Jarvis will address this more specifically.
