But in short, his actions can speak only to his having and sharing the intention to kill, not only of someone who -- who knows and assists or, as I think the submission was today, sort of a moral support, mere-presence person. In conclusion, Your Honours, his fourth ground should be dismissed. Finally, as I've mentioned before, since his arguments on the fifth ground, which is inhumane acts committed on the survivors, VG14 and 32, since they piggyback on the arguments in his fourth ground, we ask that the fifth ground should also be dismissed. That completes my submissions on grounds 1 through 5, and of course I'm happy to answer questions now or later.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I certainly don't want to read through another three pages of transcript of evidence. But if Your Honours look through at actual conversation and the

And the reading of it, if -- and as the Trial Chamber obviously also read it -- is that Stanko told him that workers from both his factory and Varda were being taken out and mistreated. utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Essentially, the arguments that the appellant raises in his sixth ground of appeal, concerning persecution as a crime against humanity, and his seventh ground of appeal relating to his individual criminal responsibility reflect one cross-cutting theme, that is, how can a Trial Chamber infer on the evidence adduced before it that an accused person has the requisite mens rea to be found guilty as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise to persecute? The permissible parameters for inferring criminal intent have been, and of course will be, a prominent feature of many of the appeals that come before this Chamber. In the absence of a confession or declaratory statement the accused's state of mind in the time in question when the acts were committed can only be inferred from the surrounding circumstances. This principle applies equally to proof of specific intent crimes, such as persecution. Inferring intent from circumstantial evidence in no way diminishes the Prosecution's obligation to prove the mental state required for the specified crime. It simply recognises that in most cases the Prosecution must necessarily resort to objective factors in order to prove the subjective state of mind of the accused. As Your Honour Judge Shahabuddeen has recently stated in the Krnojelac appeal judgement, the task of the Prosecution is rightly heavy. It should not be made unmanageably so. Recognising the heavy burden on the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber in the present case acknowledged at paragraph 68 of the trial judgement that where the Prosecution relies on proof of state of mind by inference, that inference must be the only reasonable inference available on the evidence. In this case, the Trial Chamber was satisfied that the only reasonable inference was that Mr. Vasiljevic was a participant in a joint criminal enterprise to commit persecution. On appeal, the appellant bears the burden of demonstrating that the Trial Chamber erroneously disregarded another reasonable inference that was available on the evidence. In order to assess the Trial Chamber's conclusion that Mr. Vasiljevic was guilty of persecution, Your Honours will need to consider three primary questions: First, what is the requisite mens rea for participation in a joint criminal enterprise to persecute? Second: Has the appellant demonstrated any error in the Trial Chamber's conclusion that he was a participant in a joint criminal enterprise to murder? And third: Has the appellant demonstrated any error in the Trial Chamber's conclusion that he shared the discriminatory intent of the other three perpetrators in the joint criminal enterprise?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. My apologies. Overwhelmingly, the arguments the appellant raises in a bid to demonstrate errors on the Trial Chamber's part are based on a misapprehension of the trial judgement, are contrary to the existing jurisprudence, or are simply unsustainable. Turning then to the first key question: What is the requisite mens rea for participation in a joint criminal enterprise to persecute? The facts of this case raise in the parlance of the Tadic Appeals Chamber a category 1 joint criminal enterprise, as Mr. Knoops has also acknowledged today. Indeed, it's difficult to imagine a more classic or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. straightforward scenario than the present case for the application of this doctrine of responsibility. The relevant mens rea requirement is uncontroversial. According to the Tadic Appeals Chamber, at paragraph 228, to establish responsibility in a category 1 joint criminal enterprise the Prosecution must prove that the accused shared with the other participants the intent to commit the agreed crime. In this case, the agreed crime was murder or more precisely murder on religious or political grounds. Consequently, it was necessary for the Trial Chamber to determine not only whether Mr. Vasiljevic shared the intent of the other three perpetrators to kill but also whether he shared their intent to commit their crimes on political or religious grounds. As recently confirmed in the Krnojelac appeal judgement, at paragraph 185, in order to satisfy the mens rea requirement for persecution, the Prosecution must prove that the violation of the victim's rights was carried out deliberately with the intention to discriminate on one of the listed grounds in Article 5(h) of the Statute, specifically race, religion, or politics. Turning then to the second key question: Has the appellant demonstrated an error in the Trial Chamber's conclusion that he was a participant in a joint criminal enterprise to murder? As Your Honours have rightly noted, in his sixth and seventh grounds of appeal the appellant has raised a number of arguments that overlap with the issues he's raised in his fourth and fifth grounds of appeal and which have been dealt with by my colleague, Ms. Brady. I won't repeat the comprehensive analysis of the Trial Chamber's findings that she has presented. I'll simply just refer to them and focus specifically on the additional arguments that the appellant raises in his sixth and seventh grounds of appeal. I refer in particular to the factors that led the Trial Chamber to the inescapable conclusion that Mr. Vasiljevic shared the intention of the other three perpetrators to murder the men at the Drina River. Most important amongst these factors was, of course, the very nature of his participation on the 7th of June, 1992. Given the facts as found by the Trial Chamber, what possible inference is available other than that the accused intended the murder of the seven Muslim men? Certainly those facts are entirely inconsistent with Mr. Vasiljevic's claim that he was simply an unwilling Witness to this unfolding violation of human life. None of the arguments the appellant raises in his sixth or seventh ground of appeal undermine the Trial Chamber's conclusion that he did share the intent of the other three perpetrators to kill. The Prosecution emphasises that contrary to the argument raised in the appellant's brief, the Trial Chamber did not infer his intent to murder solely on the basis that he did nothing to stop Milan Lukic or any of the other perpetrators. Certainly this was one relevant factor to consider. In combination with all of the other factors, most notably, Mr. Vasiljevic's positive actions in providing assistance to guard at gunpoint the Muslim captives en route to their deaths. The appellant has also argued that it was just a ten-minute drive from the Vilina Vlas Hotel down to the point at Sase where the cars stopped and that the short duration of the events precludes any possibility of inferring he shared the intent of the other perpetrators. In fact, as Your Honour Judge Shahabuddeen has rightly elucidated, Mr. Vasiljevic's participation in the events also consisted of the three- to four-minute walk during which the appeallant escorted the victims at gunpoint through difficult terrain right down to the brink of the river. Even on his own version of events, he knew throughout that entire walk that the men were to be killed. Whether the time involved was five minutes or five hours, the inference to be drawn from his unequivocal participation in the murder plan is the same; he intended that the men would be killed. The appellant has also argued that the Trial Chamber erred in finding the requisite common plan for a joint criminal enterprise. This argument is contrary to the existing jurisprudence of this Tribunal. As the Tadic Appeals Chamber has noted at paragraph 227, the common plan or purpose may of course be inferred from the very fact that a plurality of persons acts in unison to put into effect a particular crime. That is exactly what the Trial Chamber found in the present case. The way the events unfolded leads to the inescapable inference that there was an understanding amounting to an agreement that these men would be killed. As the Appeals Chamber has stated in the Furundzija case, where the act of one accused contributes to the purpose of the other and both acted simultaneously in the same place and within full view of each other over a prolonged period of time, the argument that there was no common purpose is plainly unsustainable. That's at paragraph 37 of the Furundzija appeal judgement. Insofar as the appellant relies on analogies with the recent Simic trial judgement to sustain his claim that he was not a participant in a joint criminal enterprise, the analogy in the Prosecution's submission is simply inapposite. The Simic case that the findings referred to in the particular by the appellant referred to Mr. Simic's alleged involvement in crimes of unlawful arrest and detention. The Trial Chamber noted that there was no evidence of his participation in these crimes, that the most that could be said was that he was at times present at the sites where the victims were being unlawfully detained. This is entirely different to the present case, where the Trial Chamber specifically found that Mr. Vasiljevic actually participated in the criminal conduct in three ways, as my colleague Ms. Brady has outlined. It is not a case as might be suggested in the submissions for the appellant of guilt on the basis of mere presence at the scene of the crime. He was actively participating and was found guilty on that basis. The appellant has also argued this morning on the basis of the Kvocka trial judgement, and in particular has indicated that this case stands for the proposition that a substantial contribution is required to a joint criminal enterprise. Your Honours, the Prosecution points out that the comments made in the Kvocka trial judgement were of course dealing specifically with a category 2 joint criminal enterprise, a category that is not directly raised on the facts of this case. And in particular, the Kvocka Trial Chamber was concerned to delineate the limits at which somebody who has an association with a system of ill-treatment could be brought within the net of criminal responsibility. The Trial Chamber was specifically considering at what point could someone employed, for example, as a cleaner in a concentration camp incur responsibility pursuant to joint criminal enterprise theory. Once again, Your Honours, that scenario is entirely different to the case that we have here, where Mr. Vasiljevic consciously and willingly made a decision to participate and contribute to the deaths of these seven Muslim men. A question has also been raised as to whether the appropriate classification for Mr. Vasiljevic's responsibility was as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise or whether an aider and abettor would not be a more appropriate label to attach to him. Your Honours, the answer to this question is simple and is directly reflected in the jurisprudence of the Appeals Chamber in the Ojdanic joint criminal enterprise decision. Once the Trial Chamber was satisfied that he shared the intent of the other three perpetrators to kill, it is appropriate for him to be classified as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise and not as an aider and abettor where mere knowledge of the crimes being committed by the others would be sufficient. Your Honours, moving, then, to the third key question for your consideration: How did the Trial Chamber infer that the appellant was acting with the requisite discriminatory intent and has the appellant demonstrated an error in the Trial Chamber's reasoning in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and Your Honours. Your Honours, I was just about to move to the third key question that I'd proposed for your consideration, and that concerns the proof of discriminatory intent required for persecution. The Krnojelac Appeals Chamber has recently provided specific guidance as to the permissible parameters for inferring discriminatory intent for persecution. The Appeals Chamber in particular emphasised that the discriminatory nature of an attack characterised as a widespread or systematic attack for the purposes of a crime against humanity generally is not for itself a sufficient basis upon which to infer that a particular act carried out in the course of that attack was also committed with discriminatory intent. Nonetheless, the general context is a relevant factor provided, in the Appeals Chamber's words, "circumstances surrounding the commission of the alleged acts substantiate the existence of such intent." That's at paragraph 184 of the Krnojelac appeal judgement. So while the general discriminatory nature of an attack characterised as a widespread or systematic attack is not of itself sufficient proof of discriminatory intent, it nevertheless provides an important lens through which to view and assess the particular acts alleged against the accused. The Appeals Chamber also emphasised as paragraph 186 of the Krnojelac judgement that if the acts in issue were clearly related to the discriminatory widespread and systematic attack, then it may be inferred that the treatment meted out was a consequence of that policy. In the present case, the Trial Chamber's approach conforms in all material respects with the methodology laid down by the Krnojelac Appeals Chamber. The Trial Chamber specifically emphasised that it had to be satisfied that Mr. Vasiljevic was acting in discriminatory intent during the Drina River incident and that it wasn't sufficient that these crimes simply occurred within the context of the broader discriminatory attack in Visegrad. That's at paragraph 249 of the trial judgement. Nonetheless, the link between the Drina River incident and the wider attack and particularly Mr. Vasiljevic's role in that wider attack was a relevant factor to consider in assessing his mental state on the 7th of June, 1992. The Trial Chamber was satisfied that in providing information to the group led by Milan Lukic, the accused shared the intention of that group to persecute the local Muslim civilians on religious or political grounds. That's at paragraph 251 of the trial judgement. In coming to this conclusion, the Trial Chamber specifically relied on Mr. Vasiljevic's comment at Sase on the 7th of June, 1992 when he pointed out to Milan Lukic a nearby house belonging to a Muslim family. That's at footnote 148 of the trial judgement. This finding is particularly important because it starkly illustrates the connection between the broader discriminatory attack in Visegrad, Mr. Vasiljevic's role within that broader attack, and the events of 7 June 1992. The Trial Chamber then looked specifically at the circumstances surrounding the Drina River crimes and concluded that the only reasonable inference was that the seven Muslim men were argued on political or religious grounds. As the Prosecution noted at paragraph 7.9 of its response brief, in this case there was a widespread and systematic attack being carried out on a discriminatory basis against the non-Serb population of Visegrad. The appellant was a participant in that widespread and systematic attack, and the Drina River crimes were committed in the course of that attack. The seven victims of the crime fell within the group targeted by the widespread and systematic attack, and the crime was an act of the type being committed in furtherance of the widespread and systematic attack. In addition to the obvious links between the Drina River events and the broader discriminatory context, there was other evidence on the trial record that supports the Trial Chamber's finding of discriminatory intent. In particular, the Trial Chamber accepted that the seven Muslim men were taunted with ethnic slurs just before they were shot. That's at paragraph 276 of the trial judgement. This fact aptly conveys the discriminatory context in which these crimes took place. Against the backdrop of the prevailing circumstances in which the perpetrators and the victims found themselves on the banks of the Drina River on the 7th of June, 1992, the notion that it was simply a coincidence that all of the victims were Muslim and that all of the perpetrators were Bosnian Serbs cannot be sustained. What other reasonable inference could be drawn than that the only reason for the appellant's participation in violating the rights of these seven men was their membership of a political or religious group? The appellant suggests that discriminatory intent on his part is negated by the fact that he was not personally involved in selecting the seven Muslim men initially. In presenting these arguments, the Prosecution submits that the appellant adopts an overly literal interpretation of what it means to single out the men. It does not mean only the initial capture of the men from their homes, but also the decision to subject them to crimes, and this decision can obviously be made on an ongoing basis well after the men were initially removed from their homes. The argument presented by the appellant is tantamount to saying that if the contribution rendered by a participant in a joint criminal enterprise to persecute occurs partway through the execution of the crimes or the criminal plan, the accused must be exonerated. Well, this would undermine the very essence of joint criminal enterprise responsibility, which is based on the concept that liability is incurred notwithstanding that the accused may not have participated in every single aspect of crime. The position advanced by the appellant also suggests that the only basis on which discriminatory intent can be inferred is the participation of the accused in the process of initially selecting the victims. This is clearly not correct. Discriminatory intent can also be inferred, as in this case, from the ongoing participation of the accused in a crime in full knowledge of the discriminatory grounds on which it's being committed. The permissibility of inferring discriminatory intent from the accused's knowing participation was addressed by the Trial Chamber in the Kvocka case. There the Trial Chamber noted at paragraph 201 that Trial Chambers have repeatedly inferred discriminatory intent from the perpetrator's willful or knowing participation in a campaign of systematic abuse against a specific group. And the Kvocka Trial Chamber referred no particular to the Kupreskic and Kordic cases as examples. To that could be added the Krstic trial judgement at paragraph 618, and the Simic Trial Chamber, at paragraph 51, has more recently endorsed this same approach. The appellant has also argued that he was convicted on the basis of a single incident and that it is impermissible to attach the label of persecution to a single incident. I'll be very brief on this point, Your Honours. It is contrary to the existing jurisprudence of the Tribunal which clearly recognises that persecution can be constituted by reference to one single underlying act. Indeed, the Kupreskic trial judgement, at paragraph 624, which endorses this principle, specifically gave the example of the murder of a single Muslim person in the former Yugoslavia occurring as part of the widespread or systematic persecutory attack provided the intent was clearly to kill the victim because he was a Muslim. The Prosecution submits that is precisely the case that we have here. It also must be said that while Mr. Vasiljevic was convicted of a single incident, it certainly was not an isolated incident when viewed in the proper context of his role in the broader attack. In conclusion, Your Honours, many scenarios could be envisaged where proof of the specific intent required for joint criminal enterprise responsibility to persecute would be a complicated question. In the Prosecution's respectful submission, this case is not among them. There are clear links between the Drina River crimes and the broader discriminatory attack against the non-Serbs in Visegrad, an attack so successful, that as the Trial Chamber noted at paragraph 56 of the judgement, the changes in ethnic composition in Visegrad municipality after these events are second only to the changes that occurred in Srebrenica. The Trial Chamber, having heard all of the evidence, had no doubt that the only reasonable inference was that Mr. Vasiljevic was a participant in a joint criminal enterprise to persecute. The appellant has raised no argument on appeal that challenges the validity of the Trial Chamber's conclusion in that regard. Your Honours, that completes my submissions. If you have any questions, I'd be happy to assist you now, or if you prefer to wait, we can deal with them at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will address you on he appellant's arguments regarding sentencing. Your Honours, the appellant raises a variety of arguments with regard to sentencing. Most of these arguments have been comprehensively addressed in our response brief, and for the purposes of this hearing we just wish to address those mentioned by you or by the appellant this morning. Your Honours, with regard to the appellant's argument about the issues of verbal abuse and the double use of trauma, we would like to refer you to the Prosecution trial brief in order to save time. The first argument which the Prosecution would like to address in more detail concerns the appellant's allegation that the Trial Chamber used discriminatory intent twice; once to find the elements of persecution and then a second time in order to aggravate the global sentence. The Prosecution states that this argument was not raised in the appellant's Notice of Appeal and that the appellant has not applied for leave to amend this Notice of Appeal. The argument should be dismissed on this basis. Alternatively, the Prosecution submits that the appellant's arguments are without merit. In that regard, the Prosecution agrees that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. it would constitute an error had the Trial Chamber used discriminatory intent as an aggravating circumstance to increase the global sentence. The Prosecution is, however, of the view that the Trial Chamber did not commit this error. In fact, the Trial Chamber explicitly stated that it considered discriminatory intent as an aggravating factor only with regard to the war crime of murder but not for the crime against humanity of persecution based upon acts of murder. Moreover, the Trial Chamber itself made clear that an accused must not be punished for the same conduct twice. To assume that the Trial Chamber used discriminatory intent twice would be tantamount to assuming that the Trial Chamber disregarded the very principle it just established. The Prosecution submits that there is a sound reason why the Trial Chamber mentioned discriminatory intent as an aggravating factor for the war crime of murder despite the fact that it cannot aggravate the global sentence. The reason is that every conviction should stand on its own. Consequently aggravating circumstances must be considered for every crime separately. As discriminatory intent is an aggravating circumstance for the war crime of murder, the Trial Chamber had to regard this fact. In conclusion, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber did not use discriminatory intent twice and therefore did not commit an error. The next argument we would like to address regards the method of killing. In this regard, the appellant's argument is not entirely clear. However, the Prosecution assumes that one of the appellant's arguments is that the Trial Chamber used the cold-bloodedness of the crime impermissibly cumulative with a factor that had been considered earlier, namely that the crime was executed in a very efficient manner. The appellant appears to consider that both the efficiency and the cold-bloodedness in the end concern the same thing, namely the method of killing. The appellant therefore seems to argue that the Trial Chamber, by using efficiency and cold-bloodedness, used the method of killing twice against the appellant. The Prosecution is of the view that the appellant's assumption is incorrect. Although it may be not entirely clear from the response brief, it is our position that efficiency and cold-bloodedness are not the same. The Trial Chamber based its consideration of aggravating circumstances on different findings. The efficiency of the crime was based upon the fact that the crime was planned so as to require as little effort as possible. Victims were shot at the banks of the Drina River in order to save the effort to have to bury them. In contrast, the Chamber based its consideration regarding the cold-bloodedness of its finding -- excuse me. In contrast, the Chamber based its consideration regarding the cold-bloodedness on its finding that the perpetrators discussed whether to shoot individually or in bursts where the victims could actually hear them. This shows the utter lack of empathy of the perpetrators. Because the Trial Chamber based its consideration of cold-bloodedness and the efficiency on different factual findings, the Prosecution submits that efficiency and cold-bloodedness are not the same that and the Trial Chamber therefore did not err. The next issue we would like to address very shortly is the appellant's claim that at the time of the Drina River incident his responsibility was diminished; in other words, that he did not know wrong from right. The Prosecution would first like to note that none of the appellant's arguments regarding his responsibility are new. The Trial Chamber was aware of them and it dismissed them. In fact, the Prosecution submits there is no evidence to prove on the balance of probabilities that the appellant's responsibility was diminished at the time of the Drina River killings. Moreover, the appellant himself stated at page 2131 of the transcript that he -- that even his alcohol problem did not prevent him from recognising the wrongfulness of the events. The Prosecution submits that the appellant at trial did not establish that his responsibility was diminished and that the Trial Chamber therefore was not unreasonable to find accordingly. As regards the arguments that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that the appellant did not show any remorse and the argument that the appellant had no opportunity to surrender, and that the Trial Chamber somehow should have taken this into consideration, we would as well like to refer Your Honours to our response. An issue we would like to address a little more in detail is the appellant's claim that he was not given sufficient credit for cooperation. In that regard, the Trial Chamber found that the appellant's statements revealed nothing or very little that was not already known. The Trial Chamber also found that it is the content of the statement that is relevant for the mitigation. The appellant does not assert that he gave useful information to the Prosecution. He merely states that he made efforts to do so. The [Microphone not activated] The Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: -- To cooperate is either irrelevant or of very little weight. In the present case, the Trial Chamber has given some but not very much weight to the -- thank you. The Trial Chamber has given some but not very much weight to the appellant's limited efforts to assist the Prosecution. The appellant has advanced no argument that the Trial Chamber was unreasonable in exercising its discretion in this manner. The Prosecution will now turn very shortly to the appellant's argument that his low position in hierarchy and his role in the crime was not given sufficient weight by the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber did take into consideration that the appellant was low in hierarchy and that he did not part -- take part in the planning of the crime. The appellant in that regard merely claims that the Trial Chamber should have given more weight to these factors. However, as stated in the response brief, the Prosecution is of the view that the appellant did not show any discernible error in the Trial Chamber's exercise of its sentencing discretion. The penultimate issue we would like to address is the appellant's argument that he should have been given credit because he behaved very well and indeed was a model detainee in the Detention Unit. In support of this argument, the appellant wishes to forward a letter from the Detention Unit to the Registrar of this Tribunal. The appellant mentions this letter for the first time in his reply. The Prosecution submits that the letter is not admissible in the present proceedings. The Prosecution will not expand upon the problem that the issue has been raised for the first time in the reply or that the appellant failed to file a motion under Rule 115 regarding this evidence. Rather, the Prosecution submits that even had the appellant filed a 115 motion, the admission of the -- excuse me, for the admission of the letter, the Appeals Chamber would have denied this motion. The Appeals Chamber has denied very similar requests at least twice: First, in Jelisic, in the decision on request to admit additional evidence of 15 November 2000; and then for a second time very recently, in Celebici, in paragraph 11 of the judgement on sentence appeal of 8 April 2003. The reason why such evidence was refused is explained in Jelisic in a two-step approach: First, as regards the appellant's behaviour before sentencing. This evidence was available during trial and therefore cannot be admitted under Rule 115. Second, as regards post-sentencing behaviour, the Appeals Chamber reasoned that the Trial Chamber could not possibly have erred in disregarding this behaviour. The reason is that this behaviour was not capable of being considered by the Trial Chamber at this point in time. The Appeals Chamber in Celebici has therefore concluded that evidence of post-sentence behaviour is irrelevant to whether the Trial Chamber erred in the exercise of its sentencing discretion. The Prosecution submits that the rationale behind the Appeals Chamber's decision is that the relevant point in time to determine the sentence is the time of the sentencing. Any subsequent events may be relevant to the execution of the sentence but not to sentencing itself. The Prosecution therefore submits that the appellant's argument cannot succeed. Your Honours, the last argument we will address is the report from Amnesty International, mentioned by Mr. Knoops this morning. The appellant stated that the -- that this report informs that Milan Lukic was sentenced in Belgrade to 20 years imprisonment for killing and abducting seven --excuse me, 16 Muslims. The Prosecution submits that this document is irrelevant to the present proceedings. Counsel for the appellant has correctly submitted that the legal context in which the Belgrade judgement must be assessed is Rule 101(B)(iii). According to this Rule, the Trial Chamber when sentencing an accused must consider the sentencing practice in the former Yugoslavia. The Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber has taken this practice into consideration and the appellant has not argued that the Trial Chamber committed an error in this regard. The judgement mentioned in the report is a single decision. As such, it cannot possibly affect the sentencing practice in the whole of Yugoslavia in such a radical manner as to render the Trial Chamber's considerations erroneous. The Prosecution assumes that the appellant, when selecting the decision, was guided by the name of the accused. This name, however, is irrelevant for the sentencing practice in the former Yugoslavia. Therefore, as already stated, the Prosecution submits that the Amnesty report is irrelevant to the present proceedings. Your Honours, this ends the Prosecution's submissions with regard to sentencing, and we will be happy to answer any questions that you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wirth. Would any of my colleagues wish to ask questions? Judge Shahabuddeen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Wirth, I really need a little help on this, and the question also goes to counsel for the appellant. I understand that the jurisprudence lies this way, that if a matter is an element of the crime charged, that matter cannot be considered to be an aggravating circumstance for the purpose of sentencing. Well, if that is right, can -- can it be accommodated with the view that a matter, though an element of the crime charged, could be of various gradations and these gradations could well be taken into account for the purposes of sentencing? Take persecution under Article 5(h) of the Statute. It requires proof of discrimination on certain grounds. But can that discrimination take varying forms such as to entitle a Court to say, "Well, this particular discrimination was of a certain grossness and therefore that grossness could betaken into account as an aggravating circumstance"? I throw that out also for counsel for the appellant when his turn comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Should I go first? Your Honour, I think you're right. Probably discriminatory intent, when it is beyond a certain level, could constitute an aggravating circumstance, even for the crime of persecution. However, this is not the submission that we wish to make in this case. Our submission is that the Trial Chamber did not use discriminatory intent as an aggravating circumstance in this case. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I appreciate that. I appreciate that, Counsel. I was asking you what may be well termed an academic question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It goes not to sentencing. It's more a general question. Therefore, if anybody has another question before to sentencing. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Having before me the Statute, I can see in Article 7 that punishable is a person who committed or otherwise aided and abetted in a crime. I think to put the arguments of both parties in the nutshell with the caveat that we take it that the findings of the Trial Chamber stand as they are, the question is how exactly to identify the borderline between committing and aiding and abetting. Of course, related to the mens rea element we have the distinction sharing the intent and knowledge about his intent. But I recall that recently in the Krnojelac appeal it was the Prosecution itself that drew our attention to the question that maybe even in addition to the definition of commission under Article 7(1) and the three categories, one can take into account also other definitions, being maybe in a case like the one before us more helpful. And they draw -- the Prosecution draw our attention to the principle of perpetration and -- perpetration and control over the act. If this indeed should be the dividing line, then my question - it also would go to both parties - would be: Is it your submission that the appellant had the control over the act? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Jarvis will respond to that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much for your question, which of course does raise one of the -- the key issues in the present case, that being the distinction between being convicted as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise or some other form of co-perpetration and aiding and abetting. Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that in this case there is no need to look beyond the principle of joint criminal enterprise responsibility because it fits precisely the circumstances of the present case. And in the theory of joint criminal enterprise responsibility, as elucidated in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, in particular the Tadic appeal judgement, there is no requirement that the accused must provide any form of integral or causative assistance to the perpetration of the crime. It is enough that the participant intends the crime and shares that intent with the other participants and that he or she makes a contribution towards the execution of that crime. So our primary submission is that in this case we have a theory recognised as part of customary international law and applied in other cases before this Tribunal that absolutely leads to a satisfactory result in this case, and there is no reason not to apply or uphold the application of the Trial Chamber of that theory. As to the question of whether Mr. Vasiljevic in this case did in fact have some sort of control over the act in question, the Prosecution submits that it is not simply a question of looking at whether the crime could have occurred had it not been for Mr. Vasiljevic's participation but, rather, of analysing whether the crime could have taken place in precisely the same way as it did. We've already pointed out, Your Honours, that in this case there were four perpetrators guarding seven Muslim men en route down to the Drina River. Perhaps scenarios could be envisaged where this same crime could -- or whether a similar result could have been achieved, even without Mr. Vasiljevic's participation. But it would have been -- it would have looked like a different crime. Different arrangements may have had to have been made to guard the men, given that each other participant would have then been responsible for guarding more than two men. In sum, Your Honours, the Prosecution submits that this is an appropriate case for the accused to be convicted as a perpetrator, as someone who has actually committed the crime, rather than aiding and abetting it. Perhaps an example might help to illustrate the Prosecution's point. Had Mr. Vasiljevic simply provided assistance, such as, for example, lending a vehicle to the perpetrators of the Drina River crimes, perhaps at that point it might have been impossible to infer that he shared the intent, that he bought into the criminal plan and took it as his own. But given the acts of participation that we do have in the present case, where he guarded at gunpoint the men all the way down to the Drina River, the facts clearly disclose that he did adopt the plan as his own and he followed it through right to the very end. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Jarvis. We will now go back to the Defence, which will have 30 minutes to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we shall do our best in the 30 minutes available to us, both of us - myself and my learned colleague, Mr. Knoops - to respond; though it is very hard, as many points have been made, though some of them have already been covered by our own submissions and explanations, but some certainly deserve additional attention, so I shall do my best to refer to those that I consider to be of the greatest importance. Perhaps let me start with the last point that was raised. When talking about very important matters, such as whether the appellant had any control over the situation and wished the events to happen in the way they did, I will just recall something that I don't think the Prosecution denied itself, because it referred to that evidence, and that is that Pecikoza put Lukic in his car and took him to find Lukic that afternoon so as to see why he was harassing his workers, not killing them or committing crimes. There are transcripts where this can be verified. And in our submissions, there is clear reference to those transcripts. So it was -- it is out of the question that there was any reference to crimes or murders, but simply that Pecikoza wanted to discuss this matter with Lukic, this matter of harassment. The appellant accepted this. He stayed in the Vilina Vlas Hotel while Pecikoza went further to see whether Lukic was in Prelovo. And then this group of three men arrived with the other seven. And now, however, instead of this course of events, it appears that Mitar Vasiljevic came there to kill those seven people, one of whom was a colleague and friend of his throughout his employment as a waiter, and we are led to believe that he wanted them dead. It is certainly not logical. And I would like to go a bit further and explain when there is constant reference that he was escorting these men at gunpoint. VG14 did not mention any weapons at gunpoint, and especially not held by Vasiljevic. And this can be verified from the transcript too. VG32 said that when the vehicle stopped on the road, that the soldier who was in his car started to behave differently when they came out and that he pointed a gun and started to behave brutally, as he said it. In answer to a question by Mr. Groome whether the others behaved in a similar fashion, the witness said, "Yes, the others behaved similarly." VG14 did not make such confirmation. I think that in this case too there is exaggeration to say the least and fabrication by Witness 32 in relation to what Witness 14 said. It is probable, judging by their own statements and what Vasiljevic himself said, that that -- at that point in time it was clear to everyone that Lukic wanted to do something to them and that he took them to the Drina certainly without any good intentions in mind. But the fact that Vasiljevic went with them was not to guard them, not to point a gun at them - and he claims he didn't even have a gun - and ten witnesses say that they never saw him armed during that period. But he's still hoping that no such killing will occur and that Lukic will do something else, because the witnesses themselves said that along the way he asked them whether they could swim, which was indeed a strange question. However, everyone expected the worst, which indeed happened. The Trial Chamber did not believe Vasiljevic, that he verbally tried to influence Milan Lukic, but it trusted the witnesses and their statement that he didn't say a word. However, when he went down to the river, that doesn't mean that he had accepted the killing of those men, among whom was one of his colleagues from work, but this can only mean that he was hoping that this would not happen after all and that the fact that he didn't come up close, that he stayed behind in the bushes, was when he saw Lukic lining them up and that the three of them were taking up positions like a firing squad and that they were going to kill them and there was nothing more that he could do. Even if he had a rifle or if he didn't have a rifle, in my submission, the situation remains the same; he could not have played any role in that, nor did these three men need any assistance, because - I will repeat - if at Bikavac, where there were just the three of them going from one house to the next and taking out some 15 men, capturing them, arresting them, separated seven of them, singled them out, and brought them over themselves in two cars, then no additional aid did they need in this incident when it occurred. With respect to the Drina incident and VG79, if I understood correctly the representative of the Prosecution, she accepts that the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. three soldiers, or Lukic plus two, according to VG79's drawing were behind the seven and fired at them but that the fourth - in this case the appellant here present - was among the trees and that is why he did not draw him on the sketch. And I would just like to recall that both witnesses, both 14 and 32, on their sketches indicated all four standing behind them, claiming that the four of them were together. And this, in my opinion, points to their ill intentions with respect to the appellant, that is, for them to -- for him to be convicted on those grounds as well, because it is quite clear that he wasn't the fourth person in that empty space that could be observed from the other side of the river. Between the sandy bank where the seven men were standing, until they fell into the river, there was again a part of the sand, then a grassy area, and only then the woods and the willows, where the appellant stayed behind, and that is why VG79 couldn't see him, and the situation indicated by these other two witnesses on their drawings and in their testimonies does not coincide with this, and this is an indication of their ill intent, as the Defence admits, for the reasons we have explained today, they incorrectly testified that he was armed on that day. The Prosecution came out today with the assumption that even though he was in prison because he refused to act as a soldier of the TO and to take up positions, when he left and when he was given labour assignments, that is, to clean the town rather than going to the front, that he may have been issued a weapon. However, exactly ten witnesses that we have cited denied this, and it would be absolutely hard to believe that no one, not even some of the Muslim witnesses, saw him with a weapon if he had had one. Unfortunately, I don't have much time, because I would like to leave some time for my learned friend for some additional explanations, but when talking about the relationship with Milan Lukic I would like to repeat again that the kum relationship after 1992, five or six years later, cannot be used as evidence to corroborate something that happened in 1992 and that that relationship, as I noted here, was not one of a best friend. Truly that cannot be found anywhere in the record that they were ever -- that they ever socialised and especially not that they were best friends. On the contrary, if it is true that in 1995 or 1996 - and he couldn't even recollect exactly the year - if he was a witness at the wedding and that his family, neither his wife nor children attended the ceremony; there was no formal luncheon, as is customary - best indicates how much he wanted to participate or whether that was mere form that emanates from customs, rather than a wish to act in that capacity. But I really they it is not relevant in these proceedings for us to dwell on it. As for his detailed testimony, I should like to refer to transcripts that I referred to in my appeals brief, which shows that they spoke -- that he spoke in detail about persons he was asked to identify from various situations. These are all people from Visegrad or who originated in Visegrad. And it is indeed not strange that he knew those persons, especially as he testified much later, that is, many years after the events, when he also had knowledge of what he had seen or heard later on and not in June 1992. But it is a fact that he was not aware of their organisation, that he made a statement that they were in police uniforms and that they were probably working for the police; whereas, he was a member of the Territorial Defence, and he knew nothing more about their organisation. Therefore, why would that knowledge of his be seen to be such that the Prosecution is using this against him? Regarding him pointing out a Muslim house, this was in response to a question from Lukic. We'll come back to that. As for the TO -- these are the transcripts that the Prosecution refers to, and I appeal to you to review those transcripts because they do not confirm what has been said but, rather, confirm the submissions of the Defence. As for taunts on an ethnic -- insults on an ethnic basis, he is being accused of not saying anything and still less of taunting or using ethnic slurs, and he couldn't influence anyone because he simply couldn't. As for being on guard in Musici when others were stealing. The house in front of which he was, only Lukic went inside and nothing went missing from that house. Lukic asked the people to inform the others in the village to come out, and while he was telling them what they should do -- that is, rather, what they should not do, that they should not provoke others and that they should surrender the weapons -- then the others were probably robbed, and Vasiljevic did not take part in it nor could he know about it. How can we talk about him guarding the house when people were coming in and out of that house? In my submission, some insignificant facts have been gathered to form four fundamental bodies of evidence, which cannot prove what is important, and that is the existence of an intent, which the Prosecution failed to prove. If a silent agreement is valid, then it could apply to these two soldiers who worked with Lukic before that and after the event, but it certainly cannot be said of Mitar Vasiljevic, who in those days for quite different reasons wanted to meet with Lukic and found himself in this situation. I leave colleague Knoops unfortunately very little time, but I would like him to make his contribution. And since it is not possible to respond to all these points that have been made, I wish to emphasise that in our submissions and motions, with respect to the facts and the law and the sentencing, we have made our position clear and I abide by them. If there are any questions, I will be glad to respond, but I appeal to the Chamber to really take into consideration all the arguments that we have presented and to pass a fair judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. First of all, I thank the Prosecution for their submissions. And before addressing these submissions on seven points shortly, I have to note that within the totality of errors, two undisputed errors seems to exist now which seriously invalidate, in the opinion of the Defence, the mens rea for both joint criminal enterprise and persecution; namely, the paragraphs 209, the matter of pointing a gun in the hotel lobby; and secondly, paragraph 105, the reversal of the Varda factory incident. With respect to the joint criminal enterprise, the topic addressed by Ms. Brady, I would like to stress that according to paragraph 999 of the mentioned Simic decision, the Trial Chamber makes a causal link between the requirement of substantial effect on the perpetration within joint criminal enterprise, on the one hand, and the position or status with power to prevent the work of the enterprise, on the other hand. It is fair to say, Your Honours, that this argument or causal link, especially may be required when the facts of a case reveal the inability to stop the main perpetrator from committing its offence. With respect to the arguments of Ms. Jarvis, I would like to point you again to the Simic decision. The analogy with the Simic decision was not made and based on this main defendant, but the Defence relied on the position of the co-defendant; in that case, Mr. Miroslav Tadic. And from the facts of that case, specifically the paragraphs 998, 999, it may be deduced that similarities arise with respect to this accused, especially while that accused, Mr. Tadic, was prosecuted for prosecution in a joint criminal enterprise with respect to persecution. Again, may I draw your attention to a distinction made by the Trial Chamber there. On the one hand, knowledge of special intent with respect to joint criminal enterprise also; and on the other hand, its effects on the perpetration of the crimes. So the Trial Chamber clearly distinguished these two elements and said that knowledge of special intent of the joint criminal enterprise as such does not mean that a participation has been proven. The Prosecution, with respect to the comparison with the Kvocka case, launched the argument that this is only a category 2 case. This is correct. However, four decisions emerge, and they are set out by the Defence, which clearly indicate that within the ambit of Article 7 under (1) of the Statute, liability may only emerge in case of a direct and substantial effect. The Tadic opinion judgement, paragraph 689; the Furundzija decision, paragraph 209; the Aleksovski trial decision, paragraphs 63, 65; and lastly, the Foca Trial Chamber decision, paragraph 393. Although these decisions were not focussed and based on liability with respect to joint criminal enterprise, they are focussed on liability within Article 7, under (1), and the Defence holds the opinion that these arguments of these four decisions could be applied also with respect to participation via joint criminal enterprise. Lastly, the Defence holds that another inconsistency is overlooked. It is addressed by the Prosecution; namely, the paragraphs 254 versus paragraphs 99 and 100. The crux of the special intent, according to these paragraphs, should be founded in the singling out of the Muslim men. Yet it is undisputed, according to the paragraphs 99 and 100, that these men were already singled out at the time the accused came into view. The Prosecution says that this interpretation by the Defence represents an overly literally adoption of the term "singling out." Yet, according to the paragraphs 616 and 627 of the Kupreskic Trial Chamber decision, within the confines of persecution, one should satisfy the principle of legality; therefore, one should avoid, according to the Trial Chamber, an overly broad interpretation of specific intent required for persecution, to respect the principle of nullum crimen sine lege, because, as the Trial Chamber says, persecution remains the least precise of the crimes enumerated. Therefore, the Defence holds that our interpretation is not representing an overly literally adoption of this term but an interpretation with respect to the principle of legality. Finally, the arguments of Mr. Wirth: The report of Amnesty International is launched on the 1st of October, 2003. It may be not exemplary for the general practice as such, but it is surely indicative for the existence of a general practice, because that decision is not a single decision but amounts to four accused. And in view of the Defence, Rule 101(B) surely allows for the interpretation as envisioned by the Defence in this respect. Lastly, I would be honoured to address the question of the Honourable Judge Shahabuddeen addressed to the Prosecutor asking where certain grossnesses in deed could determine the height of the sentence with respect to persecution, the crime of persecution in which could be addressed to the sentence -- with respect to persecution, the crime of persecution. I agree with his view, but I have to say that, doctrinally, this argument cannot be determined via the legal construction as employed by the Trial Chamber in the paragraphs 276 and 279, because such a construction goes beyond the framework of both the intra- and inter-article cumulative convictions. Therefore, with respect to this particular argument, the Defence holds the view that this was indeed a violation of the principle of non bis in idem. Finally, and lastly, I draw the attention of your Trial Chamber -- your Appeals Chamber to the sentencing considerations. In the Simic case of 17 October 2003, where the three defendants were convicted to eight, six, and seventeen years, were not only the facts but also the sentencing consideration to a considerable extent similar with that of the appellant. More specifically, the sentencing of the accused in that case, Mr. Miroslav Tadic. I thank you very much for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Schomburg has a question and Judge Guney has a question. Judge Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the purpose of the record and in order to give a judicial hint to the parties, I want to raise an issue proprio motu, which is, of course, possible under our Rules, and this is a fundamental question that when we look in our Statute we find that the attempt of a crime is in principle not punishable at all. It's only in Article 4, para (2)-- para (3)(d) that the attempt to commit genocide is punishable. In the judgement, paragraph 304, the Trial Chamber speaks about attempted murder. One can call it an elegant solution, as it was found in paragraph 268 of the judgement, to call this instead of, as it was later phrased, attempted murder, inhumane acts, with the problem that inhumane acts are rather weak -- is rather weak in the light of the principle of nullum crimen sine lege scriptum and especially not a very specific law. Therefore, I want to draw your attention that it might - and the question is - could this behaviour not be seen in case we take the findings -- the factual findings as they stand, that this behaviour constitutes torture through the affliction of severe mental suffering in order to discriminate the victims by leading them to the Drina River and then the final end of this crime? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Ms. Brady, I see that you are volunteering to be the first to answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Well, I'm not so sure if I'm -- I seem to be the first on my feet, anyway. Your Honour, your question is -- has many parts, and at the outset the first part of it seems to be your concern that inhumane acts as such had not fully crystallised under customary international law in that it was not definable at the time of these incidents, and therefore there's a problem vis-a-vis nullum crimen sine lege. Just dealing with that, with respect, our position is that this crime of inhumane acts is a residual crime, but as the elements which have been set out clearly by the Trial Chamber itself in paragraph 234 are set out and are delineated, this crime was firmly established, in our position, in our submission, under customary international law at the relevant time and in this respect we follow the Kupreskic case on this. And indeed we would even draw Your Honours' attention to the fact that the Appeals Chamber itself has upheld convictions on a number of cases; recently in Krnojelac, also in Delalic, if my memory serves me correctly, that the Kunarac case was also inhumane acts. And in that respect we say there is no doubt that the charge -- that the conviction for inhumane acts is fully established in customary international law and there's no violation of the principle nullum crimen sine lege. And I think -- yes, Your Honour is quite correct that of course one could look at this conduct and call it many things; you could call it attempted murder. Yes, you could probably call it, as you said, torture by causing severe mental harm. You could classify it as a number of things. But I think that the most important thing - and if we get back, right back to the position of why we have this principle of nullum crimen sine lege it's so that people know what is against the law, so they knew at the time that this crime is something which is prescribed and it is the type of conduct which is legal -- illegal. Everyone knows that. So that if we adopt the principle of nullum crime sine lege, so that an accused person can, to take a libertarian view, order his life in a way such that he knows what he can and cannot do with it so he does not violate the criminal law. And the most important point is that as of 1992, in our submission, this conduct - and whether you call it attempted murder or something else - was clearly against all norms around the world. And there's no way -- no issue could arise that he would not have known in 1992 that this amounts to a crime. So in the -- in summary, our position is that it is -- inhumane acts was a crime. And in the instant case this was clearly prescribed conduct in any jurisdiction of the world, and most particularly under international law. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Guney, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, and especially Ms. Brady, have endeavoured to indicate that the appellant with Milan Lukic and his group reached an agreement with a view to participating in a common criminal -- a joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution has not specified what kind of an agreement it was, whether it was a verbal agreement or a formal agreement or an implicit agreement. One could always specify that. But this point deserves some response on the part of the Defence, so if Ms. Brady could be more specific as to the kind of agreement it was, and I would also like to hear the reaction of the Defence on this point, that is, the existence of an agreement regarding participation in a joint criminal enterprise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Guney. Ms. Brady, and then the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. I'm just reading the end of the question, because unfortunately my translation from the French cut out. But I've read it out, and our position is that the agreement, in our submission, was one that arose on a -- I think the best way of putting it is how the Trial Chamber put it, and that is that it was an understanding amounting to an agreement. Now, we have no evidence that there were words, and we can't now speculate about whether there were words or not, but for us what's the most important feature is that whether there were words or whether it was implied, whether it was implicit, the agreement was clear. And by the time they left the Vilina Vlas Hotel and then clearly when they got back down to the -- to the river, the agreement was fully solidified. I think that's -- that's where I'll leave the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the Defence want to react to Judge Guney's question also? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for this question. If the Defence understands the Prosecution correctly, then no explicit agreement is required for joint criminal enterprise. To that point we can agree. Yet according to the Blaskic trial judgement, in paragraph 235, the agreement allegedly entered should not only initially target the individual or aims to target the individual but, rather, membership in a specific racial, religious, or political group as such. And the Defence holds that the mere fact that the arguments which were put forward by the Prosecution were to be followed does not conclusively lead to the observation that Mr. Vasiljevic beyond allegedly targeting an individual was supposed to target the membership in a specific racial, religious, or political group. Anyway, that no such agreement was entered nor implicitly nor explicitly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just a small question, Mr. President. Mr. Domazet, when the victims were shot, I imagine that they fell into the Drina River and that the two survivors would have had to swim for it. So that takes me to your statement. In the transcript at page 130, Line 21, which records you as submitting as follows: "The witnesses themselves said that along the way he" - and I understand by that Milan Lukic - "asked them whether they could swim," which was indeed a strange question. Now, do you have any material, Mr. Domazet, which would enable us to appreciate how the appellant may have understood the reference by Milan Lukic to swimming? Would he have meant could you swim generally or could you swim in a specific place?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witnesses were correct in confirming that Lukic had asked the survivors whether they were able to swim, and on this point Mr. Vasiljevic did not make any observations, as far as I remember the transcripts. And it was I who said that it was a strange question that could be understood in a variety of ways. It could be understood as Lukic was asking them whether they could swim, in case they had to cross the river. It was just an indication that the witnesses were wary of his intentions. But he said clearly that when they were lined up and that the men were told to shoot individually, Vasiljevic turned away and did not look at them falling, but it is a fact nevertheless that they fell into the river and the two of them, who were not shot, pretended that they were shot and remained motionless in order to be carried by the river, in order to continue swimming from a point further on. I hope I have answered your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel. Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen. We will now turn to Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic and invite him to make a brief personal statement. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for giving me this opportunity to address you. My Defence presented the main facts. I should only like to address this Honourable Court in order to say the following: I am sincerely very sorry about all the crimes that happened in Visegrad and especially the crime at Sase on the bank of the Drina River, where I was present. I wish to tell this Honourable Court the following: On that day, I really did not have a rifle. I regret deeply what happened, but I did not contribute in any way - in any way - to what happened. I'm sorry for the families of the victims. But the situation was such that nobody was able to influence Milan Lukic. If it had been possible, that would have changed everything. I have nothing further to say, Your Honour. I believe in justice, and I believe in this Honourable Court. And I beg you to pass a fairer judgement. Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasiljevic. Thank you, Counsel for the Defence, Counsel for the Prosecution, and, of course, I thank my colleagues, the Judges. And the session of the court is now adjourned.
